💡 Key Takeaways
  • Recent findings suggest that legend has it that one of my earliest gardening forays involved a large lavender bush.
  • It has been revealed that few garden pleasures rival the velvety fix of fingers dancing along a billowing carpet of lavender wands on a languid summer afternoon.
  • Bizarrely, lavender has a bit of a reputation for being tricky to grow, but the truth is that it’s the ultimate garden rebel.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that legend has it that one of my earliest gardening forays involved a large lavender bush. As a toddler, I fell sideways into a mound of perfumed purple blooms and just lay there on my back, gazing at the bobbling petals, apparently with a look of absolute joy on my face. As a grown-up, the joy of lavender is still very much a thing. I may try to be more careful about where I stand these days, but my fascination with this sun-kissed fragrant icon is only getting more pronounced with time.

It has been revealed that few garden pleasures rival the velvety fix of fingers dancing along a billowing carpet of lavender wands on a languid summer afternoon. Beyond its timeless fragrance, lavender offers constant, lyrical movement and enduring cottage garden prettiness that seems to work in a range of palettes and plant combinations. Throw in a chorus of bumblebees drunk on nectar and swinging on those violet spires, and you can see why it’s so easy to fall head over heels for this Mediterranean beauty.

Bizarrely, lavender has a bit of a reputation for being tricky to grow, but the truth is that it’s the ultimate garden rebel. While many perennials long for luxuriant loam and scoops of compost, lavender is sculpted by lean, rocky soils and blistering sun, and it isn’t that hard to harness its intoxicating essential oils and maintain a tight, sturdy habit. Whether you want a petite purple knot garden or a sun-drenched lavender planter, this enduring favorite deserves a spot in every yard. Here’s how to ensure your plants return year after year with lush, aromatic blooms.

Lavandula spp. (L. angustifolia, L. stoechas, L. dentata, L. × intermedia).

Woody sub-shrub / evergreen perennial.

1-3 feet (30-90cm) depending on species.

Well-drained, sandy, gravelly, or gritty loam (pH 6.5-7.5, alkaline-leaning).

Sources indicate that USDA zones 5-10 (Not in the US? Convert your zone).

Spring-Summer (May-September, varies by species).

Mediterranean basin, southern Europe, northern Africa, southwest Asia, and the Arabian Peninsula.

According to recent reports, before picking a planting site, you need to distinguish between the main primary cultivated types of lavender. While all share an aromatic character and a love for gritty soil, their hardiness, bloom windows, and fragrance profiles differ. Decide whether you need cold-hardy sweetness, early theatrical blooms, or sweeping garden drama. Matching the type to your USDA zone and regional climate is your first step toward lasting vigor.

Giving lavender the right start is key to years of aromatic, low-maintenance beauty. The ideal planting window depends on your local climate. In cold-winter regions (zones 5-7), set plants in the ground in mid-to-late spring, once all threat of frost has passed. This gives their relatively fragile roots a full growing season to establish before winter freezes arrive. Conversely, in warm southern and western areas (zones 8-10), you need to plant in fall to take advantage of cooling air temperatures while the soil remains warm, letting roots settle without heat stress.

Recent findings suggest that whatever your zone, give your lavender plenty of elbow room. Crowding traps stagnant humidity around the foliage, encouraging fungal leaf blight. Space standard English varieties and compact hedges 2-3 feet (60-90cm) apart. Give larger hybrid lavandins a generous 3 to 4 feet (90-120cm) of breathing room. If in doubt, grab a Stanley Fatmax Tape Measure from The Home Depot to ensure you give your plants enough room to maintain their crisp notes and elegant shapes.

When lifting young specimens from nursery pots, resist the urge to vigorously tease apart the root ball. Lavender has a sensitive root network and resents rough handling. Loosen the outer circling root tips gently before settling the plant into place.

To understand what lavender craves, picture a craggy Mediterranean hillside: crumbly, sun-baked, and full of stones. Heavy, water-retentive clay is lavender’s nemesis. If your native soil feels sticky or drains poorly after rain, avoid adding fine builder’s sand, which binds with clay particles to form an impenetrable barrier. Instead, work in generous amounts of coarse horticultural grit, pumice, perlite or crushed gravel. You can buy pouches of Plantonix Organic Perlite from Amazon.

Recent findings suggest that also, if your soil leans on the acidic side (typical in piney or damp eastern backyards), dust the planting area with some garden lime to lift the soil pH and make it more alkaline. While Spanish lavender is slightly more forgiving of neutral soils, English varieties won’t compromise. When in doubt, build a gentle mound or raised mound bed. Elevating roots even 6 inches (15cm) can make a world of difference.

Lavender is a lusty sun-lover that doesn’t want to compromise on light. To maintain high concentrations of aromatic essential oils, these plants need a minimum of 6 hours of direct, unfiltered sunlight daily, with 8 or more hours preferred. Planting in partial shade can lead to leggy growth, sparse flowering, and floppy support.

Sources indicate that position your lavender along a south or west-facing brick wall, a flanking stone path, or nestled beside a gravel terrace. These surfaces help to absorb warmth during peak daylight hours and then re-emit heat in the evening. Just as importantly, the presence of stone and gravel can accelerate the evaporation of dew and rain, keeping foliage dry and reducing the incidence of fungal leaf spot.

Taking a methodical approach at planting time helps your young lavender transition happily from nursery pot to garden dwelling. You need to set the correct root depth, establish good drainage, and avoid burying the woody crown. Do all this, and you can eliminate the risk of shock. Follow these steps to set your lavender up for vigorous, drought-resistant growth:.

Lavender is the ultimate low-maintenance perennial, provided you don't smother it with affection. If your usual gardening instinct involves wandering around with a watering can and tucking plants into cozy damp bark, you can relax. Lavender doesn’t want royal treatment. Think of ongoing care as gentle stewardship based on its Mediterranean temperament. Give it baking sun, dry roots, and an occasional appreciative nod, and it will reward you with months of fragrant abundance.

In a recent development, during their first 6-8 weeks in the ground, young plants require consistent hydration. Provide a deep soaking once a week when the top 2 inches (5cm) of soil dry out. Once established, lavender is fiercely drought-tolerant. Mature English cultivars (L. angustifolia) and vigorous hybrid lavandins (L. × intermedia) thrive for weeks on natural rainfall alone and need supplemental water only during extended droughts. Spanish varieties might need an occasional sip when the dog days hit, but that’s it.

Always apply water directly to the base using a narrow-spout watering can. Something like the Yowon Long Spout Gold Watering Can from Amazon can help you deliver water straight to the root zone. Avoid overhead watering, which can trigger leaf spot. Of course, terracotta container-grown specimens dry out faster than bed-planted shrubs, so just check weekly during peak summer heat.

Recent findings suggest that lavender is naturally adapted to lean soils formed over weathered limestone, so its nutritional requirements are low. In fact, over-fertilizing is one of the quickest ways to ruin an established plant. Heavy applications of nitrogen-rich feeds trigger sappy growth at the expense of floral buds, and can also reduce the concentration of fragrant linalool and camphor oils that give lavender its signature aroma.

In a recent development, instead of routine feeding, rely on soil conditioning. If your soil is nutrient-depleted, top-dress in early spring with an ultra-thin layer of well-aged organic compost or a light scattering of bone meal and greensand. You can buy Down to Earth Bone Meal from Walmart for a slow-release treat. In containers, a half-strength seaweed feed is also fine once a season. While French hybrid lavandins can handle a whisper of nutrition in spring, though, classic English varieties prefer to stay lean.

Spreading shredded hardwood, bark nuggets, or damp leaf mold around the base of lavender is a mistake. Organic wood mulches retain excessive moisture, slow evaporation, and harbor fungal spores. Furthermore, dark, damp bark cools the soil surface. The secret to proper lavender mulching lies in crunchy mineral alternatives. Crushed limestone is a favorite for English varieties, as it slowly releases calcium into the soil. Spanish cultivars love granite grit for keeping crowns high and dry.

Industry observers note that add a crisp, two-inch (5cm) layer of light-colored pea gravel, crushed limestone, or even crushed oyster seashells across the planting bed. Gravel does not rot and lets rainwater drain rapidly. Pale stones act like sun reflectors, bouncing daylight right up into the underbelly of the plant. You can buy Rain Forest White Pea Gravel from The Home Depot for a reflective base that reflects sunlight back up into the foliage.

It has been revealed that transplanting established lavender is challenging. This is because lavender forms a deep, brittle root network that resents disturbance. Older, woody plants rarely survive being moved, as severed roots struggle to regenerate in heavy soils. If relocation is essential, attempt only in early spring, just as fresh growth begins to show. Never transplant in midsummer or the damp cold of late fall.

To transplant lavender, prepare the new planting hole with coarse grit and lime. Dig wide and deep around the lavender to carry as much of the root along as you can. Once settled into its new home, give the top branches a trim, cutting back the soft green growth by about a third. This takes the pressure off the roots while they settle in and helps to reduce the risk of moisture stress.

According to recent reports, pruning is notable if you want to keep your lavender in good shape. Doing this at least once a year helps to prevent splayed dead centers, and encourages flower production (and better fragrance!). However, there is one non-negotiable: never cut back into the old bare wood. Unlike deciduous shrubs, mature lavender wood is not likely to regenerate. Shearing into the gnarled brown center often results in permanent branch dieback or the loss of the entire shrub.

There are two seasonal stages. In early spring, once the first leaf shoots emerge from the lower stems, conduct a light wake-up trim. Snip away frost-damaged tips and gently shape the edges, taking care not to prune too early while hard freezes still threaten. Then in summer, after the main flowering ends, it’s time for the main structural cut. Using sharp bypass shears, clip away all spent flowers and remove one-third of the current season's soft green growth to form a smooth, rounded dome. This dome will help to shed any winter snow and also encourages dense branching.

Tailor your approach to your variety’s personality. Big French lavandins can take a confident, thorough haircut to tame wild wands, while compact English types prefer a gentle, elegant shaping. If you’re growing Spanish lavender with its rabbit-ear blooms, simply snip spent flower heads through spring to keep blooms coming. If you need a good snipping tool, you can buy Spear & Jackson CuttingSet8 Traditional Bypass & Anvil Secateur Set from Amazon. Just tuck the shears away before fall chills roll in.

Grow the right cultivar in the right place, and you can enjoy decades-long beauty. Breeders have refined lavender to excel in specific roles, from compact edging to storm-resistant mounds. These 5 standouts deliver exceptional performance, pest resistance, and exquisite blooms:.

It has been revealed that there’s no getting around the fact that lavender success will depend on where you live. In the high heat and summer humidity of the Southeastern US and Gulf Coast, fungal melt is the biggest problem. Overcome this by planting in raised beds, doubling planting distances to 4 feet (1.2m) for better airflow, and choosing humidity-tolerant French hybrids (like Phenomenal or Sensational) rather than traditional English types.

Industry observers note that in severe northern zones (zones 4-5), deep winter freezes and dry winds can cause severe dieback. In these areas, stick to true English cultivars (Munstead or Hidcote), which tolerate sub-zero temperatures. Keep shrubs in well-drained soil on sheltered slopes where snow can form a natural blanket. And avoid late-season fertilization as this delays dormancy.

Industry observers note that in the sun-drenched, alkaline West and Southwest (zones 8-10), native conditions closely mirror the Mediterranean. Spanish lavenders and French toothed types thrive in lean native soils. The primary danger here is over-irrigation from lawn sprinklers. So just be sensible about your watering.

Sources indicate that growing lavender in pots is a dream, as long as you are thoughtful about drainage and watering. Containers are certainly an excellent workaround if you have heavy clay or damp native soil. However, stick to thick-walled, unglazed terracotta or breathable stone composite. Unglazed clay is naturally porous, allowing excess moisture to evaporate through the walls and ensuring critical root respiration.

Make sure your pot has a generous drainage hole. It’s also a good idea to elevate pots onto pot feet or risers to prevent drainage outlets sealing flat against patio stones. You can get Doggy Plant Pot Feet from Amazon to elevate heavy planters an inch off patio surfaces, guaranteeing free drainage flow and preventing trapped moisture.

It has been revealed that for the potting blend, you need a super-gritty cocktail. Mix seven parts light potting compost with three parts chunky perlite or volcanic pumice. Never use potting mixes containing synthetic gel crystals. While bed-grown lavender rarely needs water once established, container roots dry rapidly. Water deeply only when the top 2 inches (5cm) is bone dry. Rotate each pot in your lavender container garden a quarter-turn every week, so plants receive balanced light for the liveliest, bee-friendly results.

The best winter survival for lavender isn’t about fighting freezing temperatures, but preventing excess slush. This hinges on shielding lavender from standing wet and gales. In beds, cold-hardy English varieties and vigorous lavandins tolerate sub-zero temperatures down to zone 5. Just keep the root crown clear of soggy leaf debris, and erect a burlap windbreak in exposed northern sites.

Recent findings suggest that potted specimens are more vulnerable. In zone 6 and colder, move containers into an unheated garage, shed, or sheltered cold frame once nighttime temperatures consistently drop below 30°F (-1°C). Give them just a small cup of water once a month. Use Bloem Plant Caddies from The Home Depot to help wheel heavier containers inside.

If you're growing Spanish varieties, bring them indoors to a bright, cool windowsill before hard freezes arrive. Once the spring sun warms the patio and frost warnings disappear, ease pots back outdoors, hardening them off gradually in dappled shade.

Propagating lavender from stem cuttings is far more reliable than starting from seed, and the results of growing from lavender cuttings can be enormously satisfying. Lavender seed can be erratic, with low germination rates, and hybrid lavandins produce sterile seed that will not come true to type. Taking cuttings ensures a clone that preserves your parent’s exact flower color, growth habit and essential oil profile. You just need to be selective about timing and plant age.

It has been revealed that the best time for taking lavender cuttings is mid-summer to early fall, using semi-ripe wood. These are stems of the current season’s growth that are firm and woody at the base but still green at the tip. Select healthy non-flowering shoots from vigorous, 2-4-year-old plants. Strip the foliage from the lower 2 inches (5cm) of a 3-4-inch stem, gently scraping a sliver of outer bark at the base. Dip the cut tip in rooting hormone and insert it into a sharp 50/50 mix of coarse horticultural sand and perlite.

Optionally, you can pop a clear plastic bag over the pot like a mini greenhouse. Then maintain bright, indirect light and gentle bottom warmth, keeping the rooting medium just barely damp. Roots normally develop in 4-6 weeks, which you can tell if you feel a resistance when you gently tug the cutting. Overwinter the young starts in a frost-free frame, planting them out into sunny borders in spring.

One of the best things about lavender’s scent is that it is a natural deterrent for most garden pests and troublemakers, including deer and rabbits. When lavender does encounter problems, it usually stems from environmental imbalances like stagnant airflow and heavy soils. Here are some of the main issues your plant might face:.

Lavender is naturally woody and develops hard, bare interior branches as it ages. This usually happens due to skipped annual pruning or improper shearing. Over time, outer branches get heavy, exposing the leafless core. While you cannot cut back into bare old wood to rejuvenate it, you can prevent it getting more pronounced. Prune annually in late summer by removing one-third of the soft green growth.

Unlike herbaceous perennials such as hostas or coneflowers, lavender is a true woody bush. All fresh growth must regenerate from active leaf nodes along the soft upper stems. If you cut beneath the lowest leafy nodes into the bare brown wood, the branch cannot recover. Always leave at least 2-3 inches (5-8cm) of green foliage intact when you’re trimming back.

In a recent development, harvest on a warm, dry morning, once dew has evaporated. Ideally, cut stems when the bottom third of the florets have opened, but before the upper buds burst. At this stage, the concentration of essential oils is at its peak. Secure the cut stems in loose bundles with bands or twine for good air movement. Hang upside down in a dark, dry, airy space for 2-3 weeks. Keeping them out of direct sunlight locks in color.

According to recent reports, standard English varieties struggle with intense southern humidity and wet soils. High atmospheric moisture traps dampness against foliage, inviting fungal rot. If you garden in the south, plant in sharply draining raised beds or rock gardens amended with coarse grit. Better yet, choose humidity-tolerant French hybrids like Phenomenal or Sensational, bred to hold its own in sweltering southern summer heat.

According to recent reports, life is sweeter with a little lavender in it. Whether you want to carve out a sun-baked border for a cloud of bumbles, frame your walkway with a billowing fragrant hedge, or cultivate a terracotta pot of blooms on a balcony, lavender elevates every space as surely as it plays with the senses. So come on, expand your purple horizons, and get ready to fall head over heels with a lifelong cottage garden icon….

6 Native Alternatives to Butterfly Bush

📅 11 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (853 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Finegardening

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Butterfly bush (Buddleja davidii, Zones 5–9) might seem like an easy choice for a pollinator bed, given the name, but is it the right shrub for your garden?
  • Industry observers note that originally from Asia, butterfly bush is a prolific bloomer that attracts pollinators like no tomorrow.
  • Butterfly bush is listed as an invasive plant by several state and regional invasive-plant organizations across the Southeast.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Butterfly bush (Buddleja davidii, Zones 5–9) might seem like an easy choice for a pollinator bed, given the name, but is it the right shrub for your garden? There are a couple of reasons you might want to think twice and consider native butterfly bush alternatives instead.

Industry observers note that originally from Asia, butterfly bush is a prolific bloomer that attracts pollinators like no tomorrow. Unfortunately, it is also a prolific seeder, easily spreading past its intended area and potentially outcompeting other plants. Even after the shrub is removed, its seeds can remain viable in the soil for years until conditions are favorable for germination.

Butterfly bush is listed as an invasive plant by several state and regional invasive-plant organizations across the Southeast. Although some cultivars on the market are advertised as sterile or seedless, their fertility varies, and some can still produce small amounts of viable seed. While low-fertility cultivars can reduce the risk of spreading, butterfly bush also lacks an crucial benefit of many native plants: It does not serve as a host plant for native butterfly caterpillars.

According to recent reports, the good news is that if you’re open to planting butterfly bush alternatives, there are plenty of beautiful flowering shrubs native to the Southeast that have both high visual appeal and benefits for native pollinators, including butterflies. Many also provide food and habitat beyond their flowering season. Here are just a few to get started:.

Sources indicate that blooming in late spring to early summer, false indigo bush produces distinctive spikes of purple flowers that attract bees, butterflies, and other pollinators. A wonderful nectar source for long-tongued pollinators and a host plant for several butterflies, including the silver-spotted skipper and gray hairstreak, it offers benefits besides its gorgeous blooms. Its tolerance of a range of moisture conditions makes it a versatile option for sunny garden spaces.

It has been revealed that virginia sweetspire produces fragrant white flower spikes in late spring, followed by colorful foliage in fall. Its adaptability to moist soils makes it an especially useful shrub for rain gardens and other sites where drainage can be a challenge. A nectar source for many bees and butterflies, it is also reported as a host plant for the American holly azure butterfly in the coastal Southeast.

It has been revealed that its fragrant flowers attract butterflies, hummingbirds, and long-tongued bees. Blooming in late summer, when some other shrubs have finished flowering, summersweet offers an additional nectar source later in the growing season. Summersweet is also worth thinking about for gardens with consistently moist soil. Although it tolerates full sun, it generally needs more moisture in sunnier locations.

This deciduous native azalea brings soft pink to white flowers to woodland gardens in mid-spring, often before its foliage has fully emerged. An excellent nectar source for many pollinators, including hummingbirds and butterflies, pinxterbloom azalea is particularly well suited to partially shaded garden beds with acidic soil.

According to recent reports, spicebush blooms in early spring, producing small yellow flowers before its leaves emerge. Its early flowers also provide nectar for pollinators, while the bright red fall fruits on female plants, when a male plant is nearby for pollination, offer food for birds. A host plant for the spicebush swallowtail, this native shrub also brings pretty yellow foliage to the fall landscape.

Flame azalea earns its name from its showy flowers, which bloom in shades of yellow, orange, and red from late spring to early summer. A terrific general nectar source for many pollinators, particularly butterflies, this deciduous shrub adds striking seasonal color to woodland gardens and other partially shaded spaces.

Industry observers note that if you’re only interested in the “butterfly” aspect of butterfly bush and not the “bush” aspect, choosing a great plant becomes even easier. There is an entire world of pollinator plants to explore, from host plants for the Southeast to nectar-rich native perennials and annuals. By incorporating both nectar plants for adults and host plants for caterpillars, you can create a garden that supports butterflies throughout their life cycle.

💡 Key Takeaways

  • Industry observers note that please email us your questions to [email protected].
  • It’s been getting cold at night around here.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Welcome to the Fine Homebuilding Podcast, our weekly discussion of building, remodeling, and design topics aimed at anybody who cares deeply about the craft and science of working on houses. In this episode, Ian and Randy help Patrick address listener feedback and answer their questions. Kevin shares a Boston Globe opinion piece on manufactured housing as a way to build more houses. Keith asks about using mineral wool insulation to help control sound in an expansive space. Rob considers building an insulated box around his attic air handler to boost its efficiency.

Industry observers note that please email us your questions to [email protected]. You can find previous podcasts and check out the show notes at finehomebuilding.com/podcast.

Ian: I hope you’re done painting. It’s been getting cold at night around here.

Randy: Is your furnace and ductwork all done?

Patrick: Tool test of cordless oscillating multitools by Aaron Miiller.

Industry observers note that off-site construction is a subject that needs more attention in the US. I’m glad that Tedd Benson keeps getting good press.

Sources indicate that kevin sent us a Boston Globe editorial piece describing why Massachusetts needs more modular or manufactured housing. It mentions Bensonwood and quotes Mark Hetzlera, a Bensonwood employee. It’s an editorial, not a reported piece, so it shouldn’t be held to the same standards as journalism. Editorials represent the views of the Boston Globe Editorial Board.

Make it Easier to Build More Modular Housing.

Recent findings suggest that I’m an owner-builder in Bay City, Oregon, in Marine Climate Zone 4C. I’m planning a single-slope roof with a 3:12 pitch and a 24-ft. clear span using parallel-chord trusses. My assembly plan consists of standing-seam aluminum roofing over purlins, 4 in. of continuous polyiso, taped Zip sheathing as the primary air barrier, and a truss cavity filled with 8 in. of mineral wool or fiberglass batts, for a target total insulation value of R-56. The interior will be acoustic fabric (a black muslin theater fabric) and then wood slats with gaps to form an acoustic ceiling. I’m not planning for an interior membrane planned so the acoustic function works as designed.

My question is: With 4 in. of exterior polyiso and Zip sheathing serving as the primary air barrier, what building science function would an additional interior air or vapor-control layer serve? Would an acoustically open ceiling be compatible with this assembly, or am I missing a key risk? If so, do you have any ideas how I might make this work?

In a recent development, thanks for all you do. I appreciate any guidance and absolutely LOVE the show!

It has been revealed that one last thing: As a former radio host, I appreciate good voices, and Ian’s is so distinctive and awesome! It reminds me of Patrick Warburton, the actor who voices Officer Joe Swanson on Family Guy.

Recent findings suggest that as a fellow Oregonian, I know the 4C climate zone well. In a lot of ways, its a Goldilocks zone—not too humid, not too dry. The climate tends to be pretty forgiving, with the exception of our frequent rains.

As I evaluate assemblies, I always define and break out the control layers to see if there are any issues. Beyond water, air, vapor, and thermal, it is good to consider wind and fire control layers. The most glaring omission I see is a well-defined water control layer. I consider roofing to be a water-shedding layer, as water can get through via penetrations, mistakes, etc. You plan to use polyiso, but you didn’t specify the facer type. In our area, the most commonly used facer in the roofing community is fiberglass faced, but aluminum facer is easily sourced, too. The former would make a terrible water control layer and the latter would be okay, except you would have to tape all the seams, and aluminum isn’t the most durable. I would start by installing a self-adhered WRB or roof underlayment directly on top of the polyiso. The permeability doesn’t really matter (more on that to come). This would be your primary bulk-water control layer. The next most important layer is the air control layer. As long as you tape the seams of the Zip sheathing, you should be good there. Pay attention to how  the roof air barrier connects to the wall air barrier to maintain continuity.

For vapor control, of all the materials in this assembly, foil-faced polyiso would be the least permeable, as it is a Class 1 vapor barrier. If the polyiso is fiberglass-faced, it is a Class 3 semi-permeable vapor retarder, with a permeance of roughly 1 to 4 perms. The OSB in the Zip is roughly the same at 3 perms. In one sense, vapor control becomes less of a concern because you have created a vented assembly with the purlins below the metal roofing. In another sense, it may be a moot point because the thickness of the insulation should keep the Zip sheathing warm enough to prevent condensation. At approximately R-20, the exterior insulation would also meet the code requirement in our area. If vapor were to pass through, it would simply get whisked away via the vented gap. If you were to put a vapor-closed roof underlayment on top of the fiberglass-faced polyiso, the combination would essentially a layer similar to foil facing. In both cases, you are fine because the insulation is thick enough to keep condensation from forming on the bottom side of the Zip. If anything, a vapor-open membrane would be slightly more resilient, but we are splitting hairs in the weeds at this point.

It has been revealed that for the thermal control layer, the main change I would make is to switch to two layers of 2-in. polyiso boards in lieu of one 4-in. layer. Rigid insulation is prone to shrink, and by offsetting the seams you will avoid numerous thermal breaks throughout the assembly. On the interior, pick whichever fluffy insulation you like. Eight inches should work well, but adding a few more Rs wouldn’t hurt, either. From a wind-washing control perspective, mineral wool and wood fiber are denser than fiberglass, so I would consider those. One wants to avoid the thermal degradation from wind washing– think about a sweater on a windy day.

It has been revealed that patrick’s point about the fire control is valid. If you were to install a layer of Sheetrock and fire-tape it, its vapor-open nature means it wouldn’t affect the assembly at all. From a sound-control perspective, you might consider applying an elastomeric acoustic sealant and/or installing resilient channels before hanging the Sheetrock. From that point, adding the black muslin fabric and wood slats would work well.

I’m reaching out for some guidance. Earlier this summer during a storm, we lost a large tree in front of our house. It turns out that a good afternoon shade tree can cover up a few building science sins. In the 19 years we’ve lived here, we’ve gotten by with our AC air handler in the unconditioned attic. But without that tree blocking much of the afternoon and setting sun, the AC has clearly been working harder this summer, making it obvious that more than a fresh tree is needed.

I realize step one is getting a proper energy audit, but in the meantime I have a few questions:.

Sorry for the length of the letter, but I feel like this has all snowballed on me and could really use your help getting this project organized.

According to recent reports, thanks to Randy, Ian, and Cari for joining me and thanks to all of you for listening. Remember to send us your questions and suggestions to [email protected] and please like, comment, or review us no matter how you’re listening–it helps other folks find our podcast.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, nothing creates a cozy Christmas atmosphere quite like a home filled with beautiful seasonal aromas – but instead of reaching for scented candles, air fresheners or potpourri, why not let living plants provide a naturally wonderful fragrance? The holidays are rich with aromas from pine-scented garlands to pumpkin pies baking in the oven, and using Christmas plants to bring another layer of perfume makes your home feel even more warm and inviting.

While Christmas cactus, amaryllis and poinsettia top the lists of holiday houseplants for their fabulous flowers, there are plenty of plants that deserve a spot in your home for their fragrance, too. Alongside attractive greenery and beautiful blooms, these scented selections will add to the festive ambience.

Think beyond the usual seasonal smells of pine or warming spices and use these seasonal houseplants to enjoy sweet, fresh, floral, woodsy and even chocolatey aromas to scent your home this year.

Sources indicate that for a traditional Christmas fragrance with unique notes, rosemary (Salvia rosmarinus) should be a staple for the holidays. This woody perennial herb is evergreen and has a piney aroma mixed with citrus, floral and mint notes that works so well with more traditional holiday scents. You could trim your potted rosemary like a topiary into a Christmas tree profile, or leave it in its natural bushy shape and pluck stems to tuck among roast potatoes or plunge into holiday cocktails.

While traditional rosemary is fabulous just as it is, other varieties can offer more in the way of holiday decor and still be used in the kitchen. Tuscan Blue rosemary, available from trees.com, has the same pleasing scent with particularly glossy leaves (and highly ornamental blue blooms in spring and summer). Arp rosemary, available from Burpee, has the strongest fragrance of all and while it's capable of growing into a big plant outside, it's easy to keep small in a pot.

Sources indicate that provide a potted rosemary with bright light, ideally from a south-facing window, and potting soil that drains very well. Rosemary naturally grows in warm, dry climates but indoors it prefers cooler temperatures and a little more moisture, so just let the top inch of soil dry between waterings. This is a tough, adaptable plant so it can be grown outside year-round in zones 8-10, or simply pop it outdoors for spring and summer in colder zones.

Forcing bulbs indoors is a fun holiday project and paperwhites (Narcissus papyraceus) are among the easiest to grow. The delicate white blooms resemble daffodils and grow elegantly on tall stems, with a floral fragrance that complements other seasonal scents well. Grown in a decorative dish or bowl, paperwhites offer sophisticated décor and delicious perfume in one.

According to recent reports, unlike other bulbs, narcissus don’t require a chill period so there's still time to get holiday blooms if you hurry, as it only takes three to six weeks to force paperwhite bulbs. A good bet are Ziva paperwhite bulbs, available from Eden Brothers, as they're effortlessly elegant and the easiest to grow. For a little more frill, Erlicheer paperwhite bulbs, also available from Eden Brothers, enjoy the same appealing fragrance and even more petals.

It has been revealed that use shallow containers with potting mix or glass dishes with decorative gravel, which allows you to see the bulbs and some of the roots as they grow. In zones 9-11, paperwhites can be replanted outdoors once they've finished flowering.

Sources indicate that for a floral perfume that carries the promise of spring, forced hyacinth bulbs are a must for the holidays. Hyacinths (Hyacinthus orientalis) smell intensely floral with notes of green growth, sweet honey and wholesome earthiness. As with paperwhites, you can grow these bulbs in containers with soil or use decorative glass containers to show off their interesting roots.

It has been revealed that bulbs need to be chilled for 10 to 14 weeks, then blooms takes three to four weeks to grow, so you'll need to buy pre-planted holiday hyacinths for flowers this year, which you'll find at some grocery stores as well as garden centers. But pop a note into your phone calendar now to remind yourself to plant hyacinth bulbs in September for bowls of fragrant Christmas flowers.

Recent findings suggest that once they bloom, keep your hyacinths in a cool spot to preserve the flowers for as long as possible. After flowering, you can replant bulbs outside in zones 4-8.

Cupressus macrocarpa ‘Goldcrest’ is a variety of lemon cypress in a unique shade of yellow-green with a delicious citrus aroma. If you feel that holiday scents are sometimes a little too sweet and cloying, this is the plant you need to balance that with a fresh, clean perfume. As this evergreen is Christmas tree-shaped, lemon cypress adds a fresh element to traditional holiday greenery too.

According to recent reports, A great option for growing in a pot is the dwarf lemon cypress 'Wilma Goldcrest', available from trees.com. Though capable of eventually growing to 6 feet high and 1-2 feet wide, by growing this compact form in a planter, you can easily keep it small enough to bring indoors as a holiday houseplant for many years to come.

Position lemon cypress where the foliage will be brushed against as this is how the aroma is released, or you can simply crush the foliage between finger and thumb for a fresh burst of fragrance whenever you fancy. Your lemon cypress will need bright light but fairly cool temperatures. Water the pot regularly to avoid total dryness, but don’t let the roots sit in soggy soil. This compact tree grows best outdoors so move it outside after the holidays in zones 7-11, or overwinter indoors as a houseplant in zones 3-6.

Recent findings suggest that scented geraniums (Pelargonium spp.) offer the ultimate opportunity to customize your holiday fragrance profile. There are varieties with foliage that smells like roses, citrus, apple, ginger, cinnamon, chocolate mint and even nutmeg. Mix and match or pair with other houseplants to concoct a signature Christmas scent.

At this time of the year, the best place to find plants is via the Etsy scented geranium live plants hub which lists available stock from verified independent nurseries. You’ll get the most out of your scented geraniums by placing them where you can rub the leaves to release a burst of fragrance. They need a sunny spot, too, as well as soil that drains well. Water when the soil begins to dry and pinch back stems to keep the foliage dense.

Scented geraniums can be grown outdoors year-round in zones 10-11, while in cooler climates they're best treated as winter houseplants that enjoy the summer outside on a sunny patio.

For a unique chocolatey aroma, Oncidium Heaven Scent 'Redolence' is an orchid with a wonderfully sweet chocolate fragrance. You’ll also enjoy the elegant spikes of burgundy and white flowers that last for a month or more. Look out, too, for Oncidium Aka Baby 'Raspberry Chocolate' with a lighter but no less lovely chocolate perfume.

According to recent reports, it's best to buy speciality orchids from specialist nurseries, and to be sure you’ll have aromatic flowers for the holidays, buy a plant that is already in bud or bloom. Akatsuka Orchid Gardens is one such nursery, based in Hawaii and stocking both the Heaven Scent 'Redolence' orchid and 'Raspberry Chocolate' orchid in bud and bloom. These orchids grow best in bright but indirect light and in a potting mix designed specifically for orchids. Water when the mix is dry and avoid overwatering or letting the mix get soggy. Good air circulation is also a must, and keep orchids as houseplants year-round.

A few simple practices will keep your aromatic holiday houseplants fresh and fragrant:.

Today we’re heading back to visit Ezequiel. We’ve followed his cottage garden through the seasons over the years, including another beautiful spring visit. After some difficult weather, he is back with another revision as his garden fills with flowers ahead of summer.

Industry observers note that I hope you are all doing very well during the autumn in the North. In my country, following the harsh and troublesome “El Niño” weather phenomenon, the long-awaited and much-loved spring has finally arrived in my cottage garden in Ezeiza.

Sources indicate that plants and flowers are just beginning to emerge, a promise of the summer that will be in full swing by December here in the Southern Hemisphere. Penstemons, salvias, irises, verbenas, dahlias, bulbines, daisies, and my lemon tree… Everything has begun to stir, grow, and grace us with beautiful blossoms, lovely scents, and fragrances.

It has been revealed that thank you, as always, for being there! And thank you for sharing in the joy of my garden.

From Argentina, sending you my best regards and a big hug.

A look into Ezequiel’s cottage garden in Ezeiza, Argentina.

‘Hot Lips’ salvia (Salvia microphylla ‘Hot Lips’, Zones 7–10) in bloom.

Louisiana iris (Iris × louisiana, Zones 4–9) showing off.

A view of the backyard perennial beds.

In a recent development, purple coneflowers (Echinacea purpurea, Zones 3–9) are flowering next to the large sweep of lavender (Lavandula cvs., Zones 5–10) along the side of the driveway. I can practically smell the lavender looking at this photo!

This massive lantana (Lantana camara, Zones 8–11) stopped me in my tracks! Here in the North, we usually grow lantana as an annual because it isn’t winter hardy. Seeing what this tender perennial can become in a warmer climate is pretty incredible.

Bearded iris (Iris cvs., Zones 3–9), California poppy (Eschscholzia californica, Zones 8–10), and orange bulbine (Bulbine frutescens, Zones 9–11) make a colorful combination in this perennial bed.

Another view of the massive lantana, this time with a gorgeous specimen crimson bottlebrush (Callistemon citrinus, Zones 8–11) in full bloom.

According to recent reports, another view of the backyard. This photo has me wondering just how far it extends. I’m so curious about the layout of this garden—it seems like there’s something new to discover just about everywhere!

Sources indicate that thank you for bringing us back to your beautiful garden, Ezequiel! It’s always such a treat to see what’s growing in your corner of the world, especially while our seasons here in the North are moving in the opposite direction.

#44521. No Need to Throw Out That Old Potting Soil – These 6 Unfussy Plants Will Happily Grow in It

No Need to Throw Out That Old Potting Soil – These 6 Unfussy Plants Will Happily Grow in It

📅 17 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1138 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Gardeningknowhow

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Once you’ve cleaned out your summer containers, you might think it’s best to tip the remaining potting mix into the waste.
  • Over the growing season, that potting soil loses some nutrients because plants take them up and water washes them away.
  • Industry observers note that some plants actually prefer leaner soil.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Once you’ve cleaned out your summer containers, you might think it’s best to tip the remaining potting mix into the waste. Don’t be too hasty. That mix could still have plenty of life left in it.

Over the growing season, that potting soil loses some nutrients because plants take them up and water washes them away. Bulky materials, like peat moss and compost, break down over the summer, too. However, reusing potting soil is possible as long as the previous residents didn’t have diseases or serious pest infestations.

Industry observers note that some plants actually prefer leaner soil. Here, I describe six plants that are capable of thriving in old potting mix. I also provide some tips for refreshing the soil to give the new plants a little boost.

Industry observers note that nasturtium (Tropaeolum majus) is a beautiful flowering plant that grows as an annual in most gardens. Many types trail or vine, making them ideal for containers. The brilliant flowers come in shades of red, yellow, and orange, like in these Jewel Blend nasturtium seeds from Seed Needs on Amazon, which also offers other beautiful color mixes. Both the flowers and leaves are edible. If you live in USDA zone 9 or warmer, you can grow nasturtiums as perennials.

Recent findings suggest that nasturtiums are good candidates for recycled potting mix because they are unfussy, easy to grow, and generally thrive in poor soil. They are also easy to grow from seed. Sow seeds in your used potting mix next year when it’s warm enough. Place the container in a sunny spot and water when the top inch of soil dries.

Sources indicate that moss rose (Portulaca grandiflora) is another annual in most gardens. This low-growing succulent, native to South America, blooms in summer and fall with flowers that resemble small roses. You can find a lovely selection of moss rose seed varieties at Eden Brothers, with a choice of colors to brighten up your containers. Moss rose thrives in poor, rocky, or sandy soil, making it ideal for containers. Plants need good drainage, so they can sometimes struggle in beds with heavy soil or poor drainage.

Grow your moss roses in reused potting mix enhanced with perlite, like this Riare organic perlite on Amazon, or something similar to boost drainage. Place them in a full-sun spot and let the soil dry out in between waterings. Avoid overfertilizing, which can lead to more leaves and fewer flowers.

Industry observers note that sedums (Sedum spp.) are reliable and popular perennials for garden beds, but they also grow well in containers. This is a large group of plants, many of which are succulents suited to dry, poor soil. Many gardeners love stonecrops like ‘Autumn Joy,’ which turn gorgeous shades of deep red in fall. You can buy Autumn Joy sedum from Nature Hills to enjoy its colorful late-season display. You can also choose from among low-growing and taller clump-forming sedums.

Recent findings suggest that the most key part of refreshing old soil for growing sedum is to add a material, like perlite, to improve drainage. Place your pots in a sunny location and water only when the soil dries. Avoid using too much, if any, fertilizer.

Hens and chicks (Sempervivum spp.) are diminutive succulents that grow in rosettes and have delightfully fleshy leaves that can be bluish-green, copper, gold, reddish, or even two-toned. You can enjoy a mix of varieties with this hens and chicks plant collection from Hirt's Gardens Store on Amazon. While hens and chicks flower, they are grown mostly for their attractive foliage. Hardy perennials in many growing regions, hens and chicks also make great container plants. They produce small offsets, the chicks, that can be repotted for propagation.

Sources indicate that hens and chicks naturally grow in poor, rocky soil, so they should do well in your spent potting mix. Just be sure to add additional material to boost drainage. The best containers for hens and chicks are shallow and have adequate drainage holes, like this Deroma clay bowl planter from Target. Grow them in full sun or very light shade and water sparingly, letting the potting mix dry between waterings.

Sources indicate that calendula (Calendula officinalis), also known as pot marigold, is a short-lived perennial in zones 9 through 11, and an annual elsewhere. Though it is considered a flowering herb, many people grow calendula solely for its ornamental value. The flowers are daisy-like and usually bright orange or yellow, although they can also be red, white, or pink. You can pick up calendula seeds cheaply on Amazon, but Eden Brothers offers some gorgeous varieties, including the Pacific Beauty Mix and the Sunset Buff calendula pictured here.

Recent findings suggest that A Mediterranean native, calendula appreciates warmth, sunlight, and well-draining soil. It won’t tolerate soggy soil. It can thrive in poor soil but benefits from a little refresh of old potting mix with compost. Water your potted calendula regularly, but don’t let the soil get waterlogged. Deadhead the flowers throughout the season to encourage additional blooms.

Like calendula, cosmos (Cosmos bipinnatus) are mostly grown as annuals and are only hardy in zones 9 and higher. Cosmos are easy to grow from seed and reward you with feathery foliage and delicate flowers in shades of red, pink, white, yellow, and orange. Burpee sells a wide variety of cosmos seeds, including the beautiful ‘Sensation Mix’ pictured here. They make great cut flowers.

While cosmos tolerate poor soil, it’s best to refresh the old potting mix a little. Then, you can sow seeds and place the pot in a location with full sun. Use a large container, as cosmos can grow quite tall. Water the seeds and seedlings regularly to keep the soil moist, and then only sparingly.

Recent findings suggest that while all of these, and many other plants, tolerate leaner soil, all plants will appreciate a little refresh of old, tired soil. A few simple steps will give you better results over the course of the growing season:.

Remember that not all old soil should be used. Disease and pests can be passed on, so don’t take the risk. Also, if you’re growing plants that aren’t as tough as those listed here, it’s best to start over with fresh potting mix. You should also replace the mix if it has broken down so much that it becomes muddy and dense when wet.

Recent findings suggest that remember, old potting soil doesn’t necessarily belong in the trash. With a little refreshing and by choosing the right plants, you can recycle that old mix and use it for at least one more year.

#44519. How to Use Ornamental Edibles for Eye-Catching Containers

📅 12 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 11m • 📚 Deep Dive (2191 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Finegardening ↗ Open Full Page

How to Use Ornamental Edibles for Eye-Catching Containers

📅 12 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 11 min read (2191 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Finegardening

⏱️ ~11 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Industry observers note that if you’re looking past vegetables, fruits, and herbs because you think they only belong in the kitchen garden, you’re missing a whole range of interesting, versatile possibilities for creating exciting ornamental containers.
  • According to recent reports, as a designer, I create vignettes in my gardens that engage the senses.
  • Read More: Best Sensory Garden Plants for Sound, Touch, Taste & Smell.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that if you’re looking past vegetables, fruits, and herbs because you think they only belong in the kitchen garden, you’re missing a whole range of interesting, versatile possibilities for creating exciting ornamental containers. Edible plants can bring striking foliage, flowers, fruit, and structure to a container, even when producing a harvest isn’t the primary goal.

According to recent reports, as a designer, I create vignettes in my gardens that engage the senses. It’s no different when composing a container or a grouping of containers. For now, set aside flavor and look at their other sensory qualities: visual appeal, fragrance, texture, and even the sounds of foliage and seed heads moving in the wind.

Read More: Best Sensory Garden Plants for Sound, Touch, Taste & Smell.

In a recent development, successful container design balances aesthetics with the growing needs of individual plants. Before exploring specific edimentals—plants valued for both their edible and ornamental qualities—consider a few practical guidelines.

Growing vegetables in containers demands certain conditions if you want a good harvest. But when appearance takes priority over production, you can make different choices. For instance, allowing lettuce and other leafy greens to bolt can introduce interesting flower stalks and seed heads, even though the leaves may become bitter and less desirable for eating.

In a recent development, containers give you greater control over growing conditions, but plants still need the right light, moisture, and soil. Choose edible varieties that tend to be compact, dwarf, bush, or well-behaved vines or climbers.

Recent findings suggest that it’s helpful to choose the largest container your budget and space will allow. Larger pots generally provide more room for roots and retain moisture longer, while smaller containers dry out more quickly and may require more frequent watering and feeding. Mixing container sizes also adds visual interest to a display. Whatever the size, make sure the container has adequate drainage.

Recent findings suggest that one advantage of container gardening is the ability to tailor the soil to your plants’ needs. Start with a quality potting mix and choose plants with similar preferences for drainage, moisture, and soil acidity. This flexibility also lets you grow plants that might struggle in your native garden soil.

Because container plants depend on a limited volume of soil, they may need supplemental fertilizer as nutrients become depleted. Think about what you’re trying to encourage: Excess nitrogen, for example, can promote leafy growth at the expense of flowers or fruit. Choose a fertilizer appropriate for your plants, follow label directions, and consult your local nursery or Extension service for specific recommendations.

In a recent development, mulch helps regulate soil temperature and retain moisture, even in containers. For open compositions where the soil surface is visible, use decorative materials such as small pine cones, shells, buckwheat hulls, or gravel. Leaf mold and finely shredded bark work well, too. Apply a shallow layer that allows water to pass through, and keep mulch away from plant crowns and stems.

Use what you have and think about growing your own. Many vegetables are quite easy to start from seed. Growing your own is both economical and a way to reduce the need for purchased transplants, especially when you use peat-free soil mixes. Choosing peat-free mixes can also help reduce demand for peat extracted from carbon-storing wetlands. Collect rainwater where permitted for an additional irrigation source. Avoid using untreated household gray water on edible crops. Incorporating perennials also extends the life of your displays. They can be combined with seasonal plants or relocated elsewhere in the garden when a container needs refreshing.

It has been revealed that the ever-popular Thriller-Filler-Spiller container method holds its ground because of its snappy moniker and reliable formula. In this method, the thriller is the dramatic focal point; the filler is a bushy, mid-level plant or plants; and the spiller—wait for it—spills over the edge of the container. It’s an easy enough recipe that most people can create something attractive, but truthfully, many fail to think much about what they are combining, which results in the massive-box special: a nondescript spiky grass towering over a showy fuchsia, with invasive creeping Jenny (Lysimachia nummularia, Zones 3–9) trailing out.

We can do better. While perhaps less catchy, think about composing your container much like you might a landscape. Consider structure (the framework); form and habit (the shape); spatial orientation (how it reads visually—does the plant have a horizontal, vertical, or some other orientation?); visual texture (is the foliage fine, coarse, or medium?); and color (is it intense, receding, or something else?). Go beyond appearance and consider the full range of sensory experience: how plants move in the wind and what that sounds like, what they smell like, and how they feel when brushed up against.

Not every plant or combination will hit all the notes, so don’t stress. Focus on a few complementary qualities. Combine the plants in your container to create contrasts or enhance similarities. Look at leaf, bloom, and seed head form. The idea is to create layers—low, mid, and upper—and aim for three to five plants that play off each other’s traits within the container.

In a recent development, are you trying to create something formal, informal, transitional, organic, or eclectic? Knowing how you want your container to read to the viewer can help you make choices about which edible plants may be a better addition to the mix.

When composing your containers, don’t forget to look beyond edimentals. Often the best containers mix edible plants with purely ornamental plants, such as leafy or flowering perennials and small shrubs. The juxtaposition of disparate plants usually determines a container’s success—different textures, colors, heights, and forms.

In a recent development, while incorporating disparate elements creates visual interest, it’s also key to give the eye somewhere to rest. A collection of pots filled with different plant combinations can feel jarring without repetition or quieter areas to balance the display.

A repeat may be exactly what it sounds like: using the same plant or using the same color, form, or texture across pots. Areas to pause are pots that may contain one uniform element—such as like plants, colors, or containers.

Another approach is to view the containers as individual components. Rather than composing containers with several different kinds of plants (including vegetables, of course), try grouping containers that each have one type of plant. This can be a powerful display akin to naturalistic block-style planting design.

Sources indicate that sometimes a container needs more. Perhaps it needs some staking for a vine, or simply a bit of additional texture. Incorporate natural materials such as pruned branches (dry or living), fallen branches covered in lichen, wild berry clusters, pine cones, grape or hop vines, dried elements such as grasses, or even small stumps.

And don’t neglect the value of seed heads—just because that kale bloom has now passed doesn’t necessarily mean you want to remove the plant; wait to see those prolific little yellow pods. And a radish gone to seed showcases its most redeeming feature: crunchy seed clusters that rattle in the wind!

By definition, a container is simply a receptacle for holding goods or objects, so feel free to think beyond the pots you find at the nursery. Salvaged and vintage items work well combined with more traditional terra-cotta pots. Take a high-low approach and use found items from your own home along with a special planter from a boutique garden center.

According to recent reports, don’t forget these irreverent options can also be repurposed in unexpected applications—that antique copper colander can go on to lead a fresh life as a hanging basket. Just make sure repurposed containers provide adequate drainage and are suitable for growing food if you initiative to harvest from them.

One of the biggest benefits of working with containers is the opportunity to modify them by adding or removing plants to capture the best seasonal foliage. While many edibles are annuals that end their season late in the year, others produce seed heads or even a second flush after cutback.

Some common edible members of the carrot family (Apiaceae), including carrots (Daucus carota, biennial); parsnips (Pastinaca sativa, biennial); parsley (Petroselinum crispum, biennial); and celery and celeriac (Apium graveolens, biennial), produce flowers in their second growing season. Their delicate foliage and umbrella-shaped flower clusters add texture and attract pollinators. Deep-rooted crops such as carrots and parsnips need sufficiently deep containers, particularly if you initiative to leave them in place for a second season.

It has been revealed that osage orange (Maclura pomifera, Zones 4–9) isn’t a citrus fruit at all. This North American native tree produces large, greenish yellow, orange-like fruits with a distinctive, bumpy surface. Although the fruits aren’t considered edible, their unusual appearance and citrus-like fragrance make them wonderful decorative accessories for autumn container displays.

It has been revealed that another lesser-known edible is a well-known perennial: ostrich fern (Matteuccia struthiopteris, Zones 2–8). Its tightly coiled young fronds, known as fiddleheads, are harvested as a spring delicacy before unfurling into the familiar feathery foliage.

Lady fern (Athyrium filix-femina, Zones 3–8) offers similarly beautiful emerging fronds for ornamental containers, but it should not be treated as an interchangeable edible. Many ferns contain potentially harmful compounds, so accurate identification is essential. Only properly identified ostrich fern fiddleheads should be eaten, and they must be thoroughly cooked. For more information, see the University of Maine Cooperative Extension’s guide to fiddlehead safety. Of course, you can simply enjoy their fascinating emerging foliage up close in a container.

Industry observers note that vegetables that you may not have thought about embracing in your ornamental containers include okra (Abelmoschus esculentus, annual), with its large pods and hibiscus-like flowers; artichokes, such as ‘Purple Italian Globe’ (Cynara cardunculus var. scolymus ‘Purple Italian Globe’, Zones 7–10), with dramatic silvery foliage and purple flower heads (use your largest container); cucamelon (Melothria scabra, annual), also called mouse melon, which resembles a tiny watermelon on a prolific climbing vine; and leafy greens of all sorts. Look out for the striking edible red-veined dock (Rumex sanguineus, Zones 5–8), with the unpalatable common name, bloody dock—it’s a stunner. Its green leaves are marked with vivid red veins, and the young foliage is edible in moderation, although it contains oxalic acid.

More common edibles with uncommon traits include delicate currant tomatoes such as ‘Sweet Pea’ (Solanum pimpinellifolium ‘Sweet Pea’, annual) or compact tomatoes such as ‘Tiny Tim’ (Solanum lycopersicum ‘Tiny Tim’, annual).

It has been revealed that alpine strawberries (Fragaria vesca, Zones 4–9) come in a range of colors from white and pale yellow to pink and red, depending on the selection. These diminutive berries add character and spill over the edge of containers.

Peppers such as the teardrop ‘Biquinho Red’ (Capsicum chinense ‘Biquinho Red’, annual) are eye-catching and tolerant of many conditions. Compact blueberry (Vaccinium cvs., Zones 3–8) foliage glows red in the autumn, acting as a foil for its partners.

In a recent development, and there are so. Many. More. Whatever you’re interested in, you can find an edimental that will fill that niche.

Edible plants offer a broader palette that many gardeners and designers overlook—choosing them for containers broadens your range of plant materials and, most importantly, creates opportunities for delight and intrigue when used in unexpected ways.

Sources indicate that they also make it possible to garden in small spaces or places where in-ground planting isn’t practical. Containers can be moved to improve growing conditions, rearranged to create a new focal point, or grouped to screen an unwanted view. They also let you accommodate plants that might struggle in your native soil or spread too aggressively in garden beds, such as mint (Mentha cvs., Zones 3–9) or sunchokes (Helianthus tuberosus, Zones 3–9). Just be sure to give vigorous plants enough room to grow.

In the eastern United States, ornamental kales and cabbages, paired with mums, are a common sight this time of year. While there is nothing inherently wrong with them, now you know you have more edimental options, so why not experiment with a wider range of edible plants? From colorful leafy greens to fruiting vines and impressive seed heads, there’s no shortage of possibilities for creating containers that look as interesting as the plants themselves.

Sarah Jessica Parker's Christmas Tree Trick Is Stunning – And All You Need Is Baby's Breath

📅 17 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (879 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Gardeningknowhow

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Thanks to her stint in The Family Stone, Sarah Jessica Parker's name has long been synonymous with the holidays for fans – and even more so now she's shared her Christmas tree trick with us all!
  • Yes, it is now possible to give your Christmas tree that Carrie Bradshaw stamp of approval!
  • It has been revealed that this underrated flower has spent most of its life being a supporting actor to bigger and better roses, or a wispy filler flower tucked into grocery store bouquets.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Thanks to her stint in The Family Stone, Sarah Jessica Parker's name has long been synonymous with the holidays for fans – and even more so now she's shared her Christmas tree trick with us all!

Yes, it is now possible to give your Christmas tree that Carrie Bradshaw stamp of approval! And, somewhat gloriously, SJP's approach to festive decor has the same sort of wonderfully unfussy vibe as Michelle Obama's twig tree, which means you don't need a celebrity-sized budget to recreate the look. In fact, all you really need is baby's breath.

It has been revealed that this underrated flower has spent most of its life being a supporting actor to bigger and better roses, or a wispy filler flower tucked into grocery store bouquets. But when Kristin Davis posted an Instagram video of herself arranging flowers blindfolded (as one does), Sarah Jessica Parker left a surprising comment: “You can use babies breath in your Christmas tree.” Say what?

Now, Kristin Davis (who worked at a florist in college) wasn’t keen on using it for her own tree (very Charlotte-coded), but she did share a rule worth stealing: if you're going to do it, then always arrange flowers in odd numbers, like three or five.

In a recent development, for me, though, SJP’s comment about using baby’s breath in her Christmas tree has set my imagination alight! And with that in mind, I asked some experts how I could use them in my own holiday decoration this year.

In a recent development, the biggest risk when it comes to stealing Sarah Jessica Parker's idea is overdoing it. Roberta Sabbatini, founder of ItalianTouch Events, states, “The main mistake is using too much. The beauty of baby’s breath is its lightness.” Morgan Brooks of Plant Style Home puts it even better, saying, “One loose spiral is elegant. Three is a snowstorm, and the tree disappears behind it.”.

According to recent reports, remember that odd-number rule? CEO of Florals Memories Nadi Melam clips her baby’s breath into “clouds” and adds them in threes, noting, “Baby’s breath looks beautiful on trees because of negative space.” Translation: let the tree breathe!

Recent findings suggest that for a spiral, Brooks gathers five to seven stems, wires each bunch at the base, and tucks the ends deep into the branches. Sabbatini also skips pushing loose stems into the tree and instead secures each little bundle with florist wire or ribbon.

Recent findings suggest that fresh baby’s breath is a diva out of water. Brooks indicates fresh stems “wilt within a day or two indoors,” while dried versions keep their shape all season and can be packed away for next year. Melam agrees that dried is “far easier to work with.” If you do love fresh, just be sure to add it on Christmas Eve.

If you don't have time for the drying process, this Bexikou dried baby’s breath bouquet comes ready to use, and its short white stems are well suited to wiring into small, airy clusters for your tree.

Sources indicate that drying your own for a Sarah Jessica Parker-style tree is simple. Bundle five to seven stems with twine, hang them upside down in a dark, warm, well-ventilated room, and check after five days, as outlined in our guide to growing baby’s breath. If you’re short on time, ready-dried bunches work just as well.

On an artificial tree, Brooks adds fine floral wire around the branch wire, since the stems are too light to stay put when someone brushes past.

Industry observers note that warm white lights, clear glass ornaments, and velvet ribbon are baby’s breath’s best friends. Brooks adds pearl baubles and silver or soft gold ribbon to the list, but warns that rustic burlap and heavy red ornaments “fight it.” Treat baby’s breath as one of just two or three ideas on the tree, not the whole script.

Pair your baby’s breath with a strand of Northlight 100-count warm white LED mini lights, which stay cool to the touch and give the soft, candlelit glow that suits a delicate white filler.

Dried stems are brittle and, as Melam notes, highly flammable. Use cool LED lights and keep bunches away from hot bulbs and open flames. Baby’s breath is also mildly toxic to cats, so if pets are around, keep it to the upper two-thirds of the tree and sweep up anything that falls.

Baby’s breath is easy to grow, so sow seeds next spring, cut and dry the blooms in summer, and next December’s tree is sorted. Will your tree look like a Manhattan brownstone from a certain Sarah Jessica Parker-fronted TV series? Possibly, but only if you resist the urge to add a fourth bunch.

Eco-Friendly Hardscaping Ideas for a More Sustainable Garden

📅 12 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (1017 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Finegardening

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • The increasingly common term “eco-friendly” encourages us to think more carefully about the products and practices we use every day.
  • It’s exciting to have such a vast and diverse selection of landscape materials available for our designs and garden improvements, but many of those options have a significant impact on our planet through their creation, shipping, and installation.
  • According to recent reports, with 30 years of experience as a landscape designer, I’ve recommended countless decks, patios, paths, fences, and other hardscaping elements to my clients, admittedly with minimal guidance about the actual materials used.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The increasingly common term “eco-friendly” encourages us to think more carefully about the products and practices we use every day. When applied to hardscaping, it brings to mind materials and techniques that minimize environmental impacts and reduce our carbon footprints.

It’s exciting to have such a vast and diverse selection of landscape materials available for our designs and garden improvements, but many of those options have a significant impact on our planet through their creation, shipping, and installation. By thinking about how our hardscaping choices affect natural resources, pollution, and local ecosystems, we can create landscapes that are attractive, functional, and potentially more affordable.

According to recent reports, with 30 years of experience as a landscape designer, I’ve recommended countless decks, patios, paths, fences, and other hardscaping elements to my clients, admittedly with minimal guidance about the actual materials used. In recent years, I’ve seen a notable uptick in clients who have expressed strong interest in locally sourced materials and in repurposing or recycling materials for these features.

Recent findings suggest that some have even accumulated reclaimed bricks, large concrete pieces, and other materials with the intent of incorporating them into the design. This is exciting to me, as designs should balance the durability and longevity of products with a focus on resource efficiency and environmentally friendly options. These creative approaches are becoming more readily available and are being sought out by eco-savvy gardeners.

Read More: How Space and Structure Create a Living Oasis.

Conventional hardscape materials have a “production history” that often comes with a heavy environmental cost. This might include the lumber we purchase, edging materials, or the pavers and path materials we specify. Their history includes not only energy and resources used in production but also shipping and transport, and ultimately, their disposal or reuse at the end of their useful lives.

Recent findings suggest that finding lower-impact materials takes some research, but sustainability doesn’t have to come at the expense of durability or functionality. Interestingly, eco-friendly options can be more cost-effective over the long run because of lower maintenance needs and durability.

Hardscaping elements such as decks and fences are great examples to explore. Decades ago, the question for clients in my Midwest location was “cedar or treated pine” for most fences or decks. Now, the evolution and wider availability of composite decking and recycled plastic lumber have created increasingly popular alternatives.

In a recent development, of course, the manufacture of composite lumber isn’t carbon neutral, and its environmental benefits depend on the materials and manufacturing processes involved. However, products incorporating recycled materials can reduce demand for virgin resources, and their durability may offer advantages over time.

Another option for traditional wood features is to seek out responsibly sourced, third-party-certified lumber, such as wood carrying Forest Stewardship Council (FSC) certification. This certification means the wood and products were harvested, processed, and tracked according to established environmental and sourcing standards.

According to recent reports, patios are another popular garden feature, and while I appreciate a nicely installed patio made with concrete, new pavers, or bricks, there are some other options available. It is important to consider the permeability of our pavement selections as challenges of runoff and erosion come into play.

Permeable pavers, open-grid pavers, and some types of pervious concrete can allow water to pass through the surface and into underlying layers, helping reduce runoff when properly installed and maintained.

In a recent development, repurposing brick or other paving materials from another project is also an opportunity to add a vintage look and possibly save money. I have a client who obtained more than 4,000 free vitrified clay pavers from the early 1900s (used for streets!) that we used for his paths and patios, and they look fabulous. Reusing these durable materials also kept them in circulation rather than requiring newly manufactured pavers.

Don’t neglect to check out the wide range of energy-efficient lighting options for your landscape as well.

I’ve also been involved with some rustic patios made of upcycled concrete pieces that were fitted together like puzzle pieces, the gaps filled with plants. Research “urbanite” patios and paths, and see the amazing results!

It has been revealed that it’s a great use of a common material that frequently ends up in our landfills. Crushed concrete is another useful material for paths. It can also be used as a base layer for paths and patios, provided it is suitable for the intended application. Again, local sourcing can reduce the carbon footprint associated with shipping and transportation.

Our reasons for supporting eco-friendly hardscaping decisions in our landscapes include, of course, preventing waste, conserving resources, and protecting our local and regional ecosystems and habitats.

While the convenience of buying readily available new materials may be appealing, taking the time to look into salvaged, recycled, locally sourced, and responsibly manufactured alternatives can yield equally attractive results.

Sources indicate that whether you’re planning a latest patio, replacing an aging deck, or adding a garden path, find out what materials might already be available for reuse. Explore these opportunities!
