⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • You don't have to be a Disney princess to befriend a squirrel, which is good news for anyone who's long been keen to woo one of these cute critters themselves (ideally without a Snow White-level singsong).
  • Industry observers note that look, I'll level with you; I know that squirrels might not be everyone's favorite garden visitors.
  • Sources indicate that yes, squirrels can actually play a surprisingly useful role in the garden and wider ecosystem.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

You don't have to be a Disney princess to befriend a squirrel, which is good news for anyone who's long been keen to woo one of these cute critters themselves (ideally without a Snow White-level singsong).

Industry observers note that look, I'll level with you; I know that squirrels might not be everyone's favorite garden visitors. After all, they're notorious for raiding bird feeders, digging up freshly planted bulbs and burying nuts in flower pots. Before you declare war on these bushy-tailed garden acrobats, though, there's another side to consider... and not just the fact that they're the birth month animal for May babies everywhere.

Sources indicate that yes, squirrels can actually play a surprisingly useful role in the garden and wider ecosystem. From helping disperse tree seeds to spreading beneficial fungi, these busy little mammals contribute more to the natural world than you might realise. And they're also wonderfully entertaining to watch, with their energetic antics, impressive climbing skills and habit of darting between trees (so much so that it's well worth adding this charmingly rustic squirrel house to your backyard).

It's easy to focus on the damage squirrels can sometimes cause, but they also provide several ecological benefits. By digging and burying seeds, for example, they can help latest trees and plants establish themselves, not to mention turn over small patches of soil.

Squirrels eat mushrooms and other fungi, helping disperse fungal spores which go on to form important relationships with tree roots, helping trees access nutrients and water. And let's not forget, either, that they are – sorry – an important food source for predators such as hawks, owls, foxes and other wildlife.

Rather than trying to keep squirrels out of your yard, why not consider making them feel welcome? With the right food, shelter and a little patience, you can encourage them to visit regularly and gradually become more comfortable with your presence.

Here's how to befriend a squirrel, then, along with some top tips on what to feed them and how to enjoy their manufacturer without sacrificing your bird feeders or flowers.

Recent findings suggest that squirrels are naturally drawn to gardens with plenty of trees, shrubs and places to hide. The easiest way to befriend a squirrel, then, is to offer up mature trees (which provide opportunities for climbing, nesting and foraging,) and dense shrubs that offer shelter from predators and bad weather.

Oak, hickory, beech and walnut trees are particularly valuable to many North American squirrel species because they produce nuts and seeds that provide natural food. So, if you have space, consider planting native trees and shrubs that offer food and shelter throughout the year.

One of the easiest ways to make your yard appealing to squirrels is to let nature do some of the work. Rather than removing every fallen nut, seed head or piece of natural debris, then, consider leaving a few areas where wildlife can forage.

Recent findings suggest that trees that produce acorns, walnuts and hickory nuts can provide valuable food, while berry-producing native shrubs offer additional opportunities for wildlife to feed. And you could also leave some fallen leaves in quieter areas of the garden, as these support insects and other small creatures that contribute to the wider ecosystem.

Anyone who's ever managed to befriend a squirrel before will tell you, in no uncertain terms, that offering small quantities of food always goes a long way!

Unsalted hazelnuts, walnuts and pecans in their shells provides a natural foraging activity. Sunflower seeds, too, are a familiar food source for many squirrel species, although they should only be offered in modest quantities. And plain pumpkin seeds can provide another occasional treat, too.

Natural food from your garden should always be the first port of call, of course; acorns, tree seeds and other naturally available foods are preferable to making squirrels dependent on a regular supply from you (especially as healthy wild squirrels don't really need supplementary feeding).

In a recent development, on that note, remember not to overfeed; the trick here is to only offer a small amount, remove uneaten food and avoid creating a feeding station that attracts large numbers of animals or unwanted pests. And take care to keep any feeding equipment clean, too, as communal feeding areas can allow diseases to spread between squirrels.

Like other wildlife, squirrels need access to fresh water, and a shallow birdbath or a wildlife water dish like this one can provide a convenient drinking spot, particularly during hotter, drier weather.

Just as you would for your beloved birds, make sure the water is kept clean and refreshed regularly. Adding a few stones can also provide a helpful foothold for smaller creatures, too, and don't forget to position the water somewhere squirrels can reach safely (ideally near trees or shrubs that offer a quick escape route).

Perhaps the most rewarding part of welcoming squirrels into your garden is watching them gradually become more comfortable with your presence. Start by simply observing them from a distance, and then try to spend a little time in the garden without making sudden movements or approaching them.

Recent findings suggest that if you provide a small amount of food, use the same designated feeding area and let squirrels discover it independently. Over time, they may become accustomed to seeing you in the garden and feel more comfortable foraging while you're nearby.

Sources indicate that even if you are attempting to befriend a squirrel, please don't attempt to chase, touch or hand-feed them. Even seemingly friendly squirrels can bite or scratch if they feel threatened, and encouraging wildlife to approach people can create problems for both animals and humans.

If you want to welcome squirrels without losing your bird feeders, consider using squirrel-resistant feeders, particularly models with weight-activated mechanisms that close feeding ports when a heavier animal climbs aboard.

You can also install a squirrel baffle on feeder poles to prevent squirrels from climbing up to reach the food. And don't forget to position feeders away from nearby trees, fences and other launching points wherever possible, as squirrels are surprisingly good at jumping.

If you'd like to provide food for both birds and squirrels, consider giving them separate feeding areas. This can help reduce competition, although it won't guarantee that squirrels won't investigate the bird feeders.

If you want to stop squirrels digging up your flower bulbs, be sure to protect the plants you want to keep safe. This might mean covering newly planted bulbs with wire mesh or use protective bulb baskets, as these allow plants to grow while making it much harder for squirrels to reach the bulbs.

Alternatively, you can also cover the soil in containers with suitable mesh or another physical barrier, particularly during the autumn planting season. This approach allows squirrels to continue visiting the garden while protecting the areas where their digging is less welcome.

Squirrels might occasionally test a gardener's patience, but they're also fascinating little creatures that play a role in supporting healthy ecosystems.

Sources indicate that if you want to befriend a squirrel, you may find that simply providing natural food sources, shelter and fresh water does the trick! And if you do decide to put out the occasional treat, remember that moderation and good hygiene are key; these are wild animals, and the aim should be to encourage natural visits rather than turn them into pets.

Oh sure, you might not be able to stop every squirrel from investigating your bird feeders or digging in your flower beds, but learning to accommodate these lively visitors? Well, that could make your garden a much more interesting place to spend time in the long run...

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that the seasons are shifting, which means our feathered friends are about to embark upon a changing of the guard... so which is your birth month winter bird, you ask?

In a recent development, it's not a silly question, by any means. After all, some birds migrate south for winter, some arrive from further north, and year-round residents shift their habits. And, from the brilliant red cardinal perched against a snowy backdrop to the tiny dark-eyed junco hopping beneath a bird feeder, these seasonal visitors have plenty of personality.

With that in mind, then, what if every month had its own winter bird to call its own? What might it reveal about the people born under its wings?

Now, we’re already familiar with the idea of a classic birth month bird, not to mention the birth month owl and birth month bird of prey, but what might the unique traits that make each winter bird so wonderful say about our own personalities?

Some are bold and charismatic, others are quiet and contemplative, and a few are wonderfully independent. All, though, are beautiful in their own special way, and so much fun to watch as they go about their business over the colder months.

With that in mind, then, I've paired 12 fascinating winter birds with the personality traits commonly associated with each birth month, along with a few easy ways you can make your garden a more welcoming place for them. Time to grab yourself a motion-activated wildlife camera with night vision, like the GardePro on Amazon, then, and start reading...

And if you love helping birds in your backyard, then enter our competition to win a Birdfy smart feeder.

If you're born in January, you're likely to be headstrong, disciplined and hardworking (all of which are, natural leadership qualities, just in case you fancied informing your boss). Naturally, then, your birth month winter bird is a wonderful reflection of that determination: the snow bunting.

These beautiful little birds are highly social during winter, often gathering in flocks to forage for seeds in open fields and along shorelines, while their ability to thrive in bitterly cold conditions is rather impressive for such a small bird.

Like January babies, basically, they don't shy away from a challenge; they meet it head-on! To help them do this, be sure to leave native grasses and seed-producing plants standing where possible, rather than tidying every corner of your garden.

One of the most iconic birds in the world, the striking snowy owl has brilliant white plumage, piercing yellow eyes and an unmistakable presence. They spend much of the year in the Arctic, but some travel south during winter, occasionally appearing in northern parts of the United States (although they tend to favour wide-open landscapes, including coastal dunes, fields and other exposed areas where they can hunt).

Often solitary hunters, February's birth month winter bird gets by on its own instincts and remarkable ability to spot prey from a distance. It's also wonderfully adapted to its harsh environment, making it a fitting symbol of independence, deep-thinking, and inner strength.

To help snowy owls out over the colder months, avoid using rodenticides that can poison birds of prey, turn your garden into an owl hangout (it only takes five plants), and always give any owl you encounter plenty of space.

Industry observers note that march babies are often associated with introspection, creativity, compassion and a thoughtful nature. It makes a whole lot of sense, then, that their birth month winter bird is the dark-eyed junco, a small but charming visitor that brings plenty of life to colder gardens.

Sometimes nicknamed the snowbird, dark-eyed juncos tend to spend much of their time quietly hopping around on the ground, searching for fallen seeds beneath trees and feeders. As such, they're a lovely match for March personalities: observant, gentle and happy to enjoy the quieter things in life.

Industry observers note that if you fancy seeing more in your garden, remember that juncos are particularly fond of feeding on the ground, so provide a sheltered feeding area with small seeds. Leaving native grasses and seed heads standing also gives them more natural foraging opportunities.

Shop Junco Bird Feeding Essentials:.

According to recent reports, if you're an April baby, you're thought to be charismatic, energetic, straightforward and naturally confident. As such, there's perhaps no better bird to represent you than the unmistakable blue jay.

With its brilliant blue plumage, distinctive crest and loud calls, the blue jay certainly knows how to make itself noticed. These intelligent members of the crow family have bold personalities that often make them one of the most entertaining birds to watch, in fact.

Blue jays are also clever problem-solvers, not to mention never afraid to make their presence known. Plant native oak trees and other nut-producing species to provide natural food and shelter to help them out, and remember that they also enjoy unsalted peanuts , so you can occasionally offer some in a suitable feeder.

I know, I know; a wild turkey might not feel like the most glamorous birth month winter bird, but hear me out! May personalities are often described as sociable, talented, loyal and strong-willed. And wild turkeys? Why, they're highly social, often gathering in flocks during winter as they search for food, not to mention putting on some impressive courtship displays.

They're also resourceful foragers, searching through woodland floors for seeds, nuts, berries and insects. During colder months, they can be spotted scratching through leaf litter and searching beneath trees for whatever food they can find. To help yours out, then, take care to leave natural cover in place where possible, and avoid using pesticides that reduce the insects and other natural food sources they rely on.

Known for its melancholy-sounding coo, the gentle mourning dove is a familiar sight across much of the United States, often seen perched on telephone wires, fences and tree branches, or quietly searching the ground for seeds.

Recent findings suggest that they're also known for their strong pair bonds, with partners often working together to raise their young, so it's easy to see why this bird suits June babies (especially as they tend to be such romantic dreamers). It's a birth month winter bird that perfectly aligns with all of that sensitivity and imagination.

Remember, mourning doves enjoy feeding on the ground, so provide a clean feeding area with something like sunflower hearts if you want to see them in your garden. Plant some native seed-producing plants and shrubs, too, to help provide natural food and shelter.

July babies are adventurous free spirits known for their cheerful and (ahem) slightly slightly eccentric personalities, not to mention their strong protective streaks when it comes to family. It was inevitable, then, that the snow goose would prove their birth month winter bird.

In a recent development, known for their impressive journeys between breeding and wintering grounds, snow geese are often spotted travelling in enormous flocks that fill the sky with their distinctive calls. They are also strongly connected to family life; young birds travel with their parents, and family groups can remain together during migration and winter.

Industry observers note that if you want to help your feathery soulmate out, remember that snow geese depend on healthy wetlands, grasslands and agricultural landscapes during migration and winter. Supporting wetland conservation and protecting natural resting and feeding areas, then, is one of the best ways to keeo them thriving.

It makes so much sense that August babies get the delightful red-breasted nuthatch as their birth month winter bird, as it sums up all their best qualities perfectly. Yes, this little bird might be small, but it certainly doesn't lack confidence. One of its most entertaining habits is climbing headfirst down tree trunks, something it does with remarkable ease as it searches for insects and seeds hidden in the bark.

Recent findings suggest that during autumn and winter, red-breasted nuthatches also collect and store conifer seeds, helping ensure they have food available when conditions become more challenging. They're hardworking, resourceful and rather determined, making them a lovely match for August birthdays.

It has been revealed that to help them out, try to plant native trees such as pine, spruce and fir where appropriate for your region. You can also offer sunflower seeds, peanuts or suet in a clean feeder, particularly during colder weather.

Intelligent, spiritual, organized and analytical, September babies tend to be more successful in life (genuinely; look it up!) and thus are represented by the pine siskin.

These small finches might be easy to overlook at first, but they're fascinating little birds. They are adaptable, clever, and brimming with plenty of resourcefulness, though, which is why you often seen clinging to the tips of pine branches and even hanging upside down as they extract seeds from cones.

Sure, they're rather unpredictable visitors, as their movements depend heavily on food availability; this means that some gardens might welcome large flocks one winter and see very few the next. To keep them flocking, grow native conifers and other seed-producing plants to provide natural food, as well as nyjer (thistle) seed and sunflower hearts in finch feeders.

Sources indicate that as an October baby myself, I'm more than happy to see this charming wanderer as my birth month winter bird! Especially as, with its striking yellow, black and white plumage and enormous pale bill, this chunky finch is one of North America's most distinctive birds.

According to recent reports, evening grosbeaks are adventurous travellers, sometimes moving considerable distances in search of food during autumn and winter. They're also wonderfully sociable, often gathering in groups around food sources and making quite an impression when they arrive at a backyard feeder.

For October birthdays, they're a lovely symbol of persistence, confidence and a little good fortune. After all, spotting one can feel like winning a small birdwatching lottery (although you can boost your chances with a handful of black-oil sunflower seeds, which can be offered in a sturdy platform feeder).

Empathetic, generous, brave and deeply determined, November-born souls are represented by one of North America's most magnificent waterbirds: the trumpeter swan.

In a recent development, these enormous white swans are impressive in every sense, with long necks, powerful wings and a distinctive black bill. They are known for their strong pair bonds and devoted parenting, and their family groups can be particularly striking to see gliding across a winter lake. In fact, it's their loyalty, protective instincts and graceful strength that make them a beautiful match for November birthdays.

These aren't traditional garden birds, so you can help them by protecting local wetlands, ponds and freshwater habitats, and always taking care to avoid disturbing swans when they're resting or feeding.

Industry observers note that generous, patriotic, optimistic and willing to take a few risks? Yeah, obviously the birth month winter bird for December is the cardinal!

Known for their strong pair bonds and the way they communicate through a variety of musical calls, their cheerful appearance against bare branches and snowy gardens has led to them becoming something not unlike a symbol of hope during the festive season. In fact, many believe that if they're the first bird you spot on January 1st, you're owed 12 months of love, optimism, and luck for the year ahead.

If you want to help yours out, plant native berry-producing shrubs such as winterberry, serviceberry and dogwood to make your garden a one-stop destination for food, shelter, and nesting opportunities.

Whether you believe in the concept of a birth month winter bird or not, there's no denying that they serve as a lovely reminder of just how much wildlife is around us, even during the coldest months of the year.

And perhaps the best part is that you don't have to wait for your own birth month to enjoy these feathered visitors. By planting native trees and shrubs, leaving seed heads standing, providing clean water and maintaining safe feeding areas, you can help make your garden a welcoming winter refuge for your feathered friends throughout the year.

In a recent development, give it a go, I say! You'll do your bit for local wildlife and you might even discover a new favorite feathered friend along the way...

In a recent development, grant referred to a house where he recently stayed as a “tiny house,” describing it as being about 16 ft. x 30 ft. I guess I have lived in a “tiny house” for 20 years! Ours is a Cape, built in 1953 by the people from whom we bought it. It has a 24-ft. x 26-ft. footprint and no dormer.

As discussed on the podcast, there are a lot of great things about a house this size. However, it is, in fact, too small. It is too small to comfortably fit furniture or closets or a family to gather to watch a movie. Our “primary bedroom” is 10 ft. x 11 ft. with a small closet out of that boundary.

The full house could be arranged to be a very nice size for a couple, but it feels too small for four of us, especially with only one bathroom. I’m not sure how we’ve worked out the lack of closet space and single bathroom with three women plus me, but we have. When my daughters were in high school, I found it emotionally uncomfortable that most of their friends had bigger and nicer homes.

In a recent development, putting my hurt ego aside, I feel they are lucky to be able to appreciate future living spaces that will likely be more luxurious than they are used to. My oldest daughter definitely had a better bedroom at college and easier access to a bathroom!

Discussion of Chris Briley’s recent low-voltage lighting article on Green Building Advisor.

What do you think as an electrician? Does it make sense to switch our wiring methods for modern lighting? Ian, what do you think about this?

When you look at a finished house, what are the small details that make you feel the builder really took the time to do things right?

I’m thinking more about the little things that might not stand out in photos but make a difference once you actually live in the house—clean trim work, well-planned storage, good lighting, quiet doors, sensible outlets, properly finished transitions, etc.

I’ve noticed that some of the most enjoyable spaces aren’t necessarily the most expensive ones. They just seem to have fewer little annoyances because someone thought through how the space would actually be used.

In a recent development, for those of you who have built or remodeled homes, what is one relatively small detail you’re especially glad you included? And is there anything you wish you’d thought about before construction was finished?

We talked about what gives you confidence in a builder, so now let’s talk about what you see most often on construction sites that is done poorly or incorrectly?

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Hi GPOD! Today we’re heading to Hingham, Massachusetts, for some beautiful fall color from Nancy. Nancy sent in photos of the trees and shrubs winding down the season in her garden, along with one of the last flowers still hanging on.

This is our sugar maple (Acer saccharum, Zones 3–8) showing off its fall foliage before it drops its leaves to keep my gardens warm this winter.

My ‘Forest Pansy’ eastern redbud (Cercis canadensis ‘Forest Pansy’, Zones 5–9) is maroon most of the year until fall, when it turns a lovely yellow.

My paperbark maple (Acer griseum, Zones 4–8) has had a hard time coping with our summer droughts and water restrictions, but it looked a lovely red this fall.

Industry observers note that this is another native tree that many people are not familiar with, fringe tree (Chionanthus virginicus, Zones 4–9), which has fragrant white flowers hanging from its branches in late spring to early summer. As you can see, it also looks beautiful in its yellow fall foliage.

In the front of this picture is a young sweetgum (Liquidambar styraciflua, Zones 5–9), which has spectacular red color in the fall and develops spiky seed balls as it matures. In the distance is a blackhaw viburnum (Viburnum prunifolium, Zones 3–9) showing its orange fall color.

In a recent development, ‘Mount Airy’ fothergilla (Fothergilla ‘Mount Airy’, Zones 5–8) glows red and orange in front of fragrant abelia (Abelia mosanensis, Zones 4–8), whose fall color is beginning to fade. The abelia will charm us all again in spring with its fragrant blooms.

In a recent development, sweetshrub (Calycanthus floridus, Zones 5–9) on the right has turned a lovely yellow. Amazingly, all three sweetshrubs shown here had the bark eaten off around every trunk by rabbits last winter, killing every one. They all grew back from the roots, showing just how resilient they are. On the left, ‘Mount Airy’ fothergilla is showing off its red fall foliage, and in back is ‘Alice’ oakleaf hydrangea (Hydrangea quercifolia ‘Alice’, Zones 5–9) with maroon fall foliage.

One of the only flowers left blooming is ‘Sheffield Pink’ chrysanthemum (Chrysanthemum ‘Sheffield Pink’, Zones 5–9), which complements the dark foliage of Diabolo ninebark (Physocarpus opulifolius ‘Monlo’, Zones 3–7) behind it.

Thanks for sharing your fall garden with us, Nancy! Nancy notes she’s ready to wander the garden, make her list of what needs dividing in spring, and figure out what new plants need to be bought. Sounds like a good way to spend the off-season to me!

💡 Key Takeaways

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

As I write this, I cannot stop glancing at my Japanese maple, its entire canopy ablaze with crimson and orange foliage. It's my little jewel of the garden, a sentiment shared by many of my friends with these small trees in their landscapes.

According to recent reports, japanese maples (Acer palmatum) are counted among the most beautiful ornamental trees around, with their elegant branching structure, graceful canopy, and spectacular fall foliage. Since these trees are usually hardy down to USDA zone 4 or 5, they may shrug off winter cold. But that doesn’t make them immune to winter damage from the cold weather, harsh winds, and fluctuating soil moisture. Young trees and container trees are especially vulnerable.

Industry observers note that so you should have more than a few items on your list for Japanese maple tree care before winter. If not, you’ve come to the right place. This guide explains the six simple but essential tasks to ensure your Japanese maple makes it through winter with flying colors. You can do them at the same time as your other garden winterizing tasks.

Sources indicate that don’t worry too much about watering your Japanese maple during winter. When the leaves fall and the tree enters dormancy, it needs very little water. Water trees only if there has been no precipitation for several weeks and the ground is bone dry.

However, to help them through the winter, give them one final irrigation before the ground freezes. If the summer has been hot and/or dry, make this a deep watering. A soaker hose is ideal for delivering a slow, even soaking across the tree's root zone without wasting water. The Gilmour Round Soaker Hose from Amazon is a good option, as it distributes water evenly along its length.

It has been revealed that tuck a cozy blanket of mulch around your precious tree in November. Use something organic – wood chips or bark work well. Miracle-Gro Organic All Natural Mulch from Home Depot is a good option, made from natural, shredded wood. Layer up to 4 inches (10 cm) of mulch over the root zone. This protects the roots, holds heat in the soil, and prevents frost heaving.

It has been revealed that don’t make the mistake of piling the mulch up against the trunk in a “volcano” arrangement. The mulch should never touch the trunk since that can cause wood rot.

Is your Japanese maple a young tree you planted within the last three years? You’ll want to give the juvenile tree extra protection. This will also be true if you live in a region with an exceptionally cold winter.

In these circumstances, help your tree survive with insulation. Wrap vulnerable trunks or branches with burlap, such as this Riare Natural Burlap Plant Protection Wrap from Amazon, to shield them against harsh, drying winter winds. Leave the burlap loose enough to allow the tree to breathe.

According to recent reports, if your tree has broken or diseased branches, the best time to take those off is now, whenever you notice. And you should check regularly to spot problems early. But aside from this type of damage, do not give your Japanese maple a haircut in November or at any other point during dormancy. Pruning at this time can leave cuts vulnerable to disease and frost damage.

Would you have an energy drink just before bedtime? Of course not. And for all the same reasons, do not fertilize your Japanese maple in November. Fertilizer, especially nitrogen fertilizer, induces new growth just as the tree should be entering winter dormancy. This new growth is tender and will easily freeze in the first flush of winter weather, leading to dieback or split bark.

It has been revealed that in spring, if your tree needs feeding, use a gentle, slow-release fertilizer, such as Espoma Organic Tree-tone (6-3-2) from Amazon. Apply sparingly, following the package instructions, as Japanese maples generally don't need much fertilizer.

It has been revealed that it won’t surprise you to hear that container maple trees require more protection than a Japanese maple with its roots deep in the garden soil. Their roots are much closer to the cold air on all sides, and therefore can freeze or dry out faster.

Sources indicate that you’ll want to take steps to protect a potted Japanese maple. A good first step is to insulate the containers with bubble wrap or burlap. Wrap the pots well and cluster the containers together near the house to attract radiant heat. It also helps to use pot feet, like Bosmere's Pot Toes, or even wood blocks to raise the containers off the cold ground and support good drainage.

In the most severe winters, you can move your container trees into a shelter, like an unheated garage or a sheltered porch.

Sources indicate that does your tree still have leaves as Thanksgiving arrives? This is normal, not a cause for alarm.

Trees have an abscission layer at the base of their leaf stems that releases the leaves to fall in the cold. But Japanese maples build this layer more slowly than other deciduous trees like red or sugar maples. And if you’ve had a mild autumn, this can delay leaf drop even further, even into December.

Recent findings suggest that this means additional watering work for you. While your maple still has leaves, you’ll need to keep watering whenever the soil is dry. At the same time, rake up leaves that do fall and remove them. You don’t want soggy or decaying piles of maple leaves since this can encourage the spread of fungal spores.

Teo Spengler is a master gardener and a docent at the San Francisco Botanical Garden, where she hosts public tours. 💡 Key Takeaways
  • Just because you like gardening doesn’t mean that you enjoy every landscape task.
  • Recent findings suggest that so just say no to digging in the fall and say yes to lasagna gardening.
  • Here, I will walk you through the four-layer lasagna garden recipe.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Just because you like gardening doesn’t mean that you enjoy every landscape task. Some of us gardeners love planting flowers but don’t enjoy raking leaves. Others like tucking mulch around their shrubs but won’t pull weeds. But digging up the garden dirt and turning it over is not high on anyone’s list of favorite tasks.

Recent findings suggest that so just say no to digging in the fall and say yes to lasagna gardening. It’s a clever, no-dig technique that works best in fall. Leave the shovel in the garage and instead, stack layers of cardboard, fallen leaves, and other organic materials over the garden soil, letting them break down naturally over winter. The result is fertile planting beds for spring.

Ready to get “cooking”? Here, I will walk you through the four-layer lasagna garden recipe.

Recent findings suggest that of course you love your garden, but wouldn’t it be nice if the garden could do most of the work of preparing the beds for spring planting? Lasagna gardening, aka no-dig or no-till gardening, allows your garden to do most of the work of decomposition and replenishment. The technique is really cold composting in place.

It has been revealed that this low-effort process works like home composting: alternate layers of green and brown materials, then let them break down into the soil. Cut grass and kitchen scraps are green materials; cardboard and dried leaves are brown materials. Your “lasagna” is a compost heap waiting to happen.

In a recent development, you can also think of lasagna gardening as mimicking the forest floor. It works the same way soil is built up in a woodland. First, leaves pile up and decompose on the forest floor. Along come microbes and worms that transform that debris into rich soil. Lasagna gardening follows the same pattern, making your garden bed into a soil ecosystem.

According to recent reports, when you make a lasagna for dinner, you just layer up the pasta, the ragù, the sauce, and grated cheese, then pop it in the oven. Without any additional work on your part, a luscious dinner will be ready when it is time to eat.

It has been revealed that A winter lasagna garden uses the same system. You stack up four layers, then leave it to decompose. Without any additional work on your part, your garden will have rich, fertile soil for spring. Here are the four key layers.

Industry observers note that think of cardboard as the weed barrier. First, weed-whack or mow the area to cut down any weeds or grass. A cordless string trimmer, like this Worx model, makes things easier.

Industry observers note that then, lay sheets of flattened cardboard right over the soil in your garden, using overlapping layers to cover the entire area. Heavy, corrugated cardboard works best to keep grass and weeds out while still welcoming earthworms. After that is done, douse all of the cardboard with lukewarm water.

Sources indicate that this is the carbon layer, supporting soil microbes and providing structural aeration. I like using dry autumn leaves (what else are you going to do with them?), but a thick layer of any type of brown material will work, giving your garden soil a carbon-rich environment. Alternatives include straw, peat moss, sawdust, wood chips, or shredded newspaper.

If you don't have enough waste materials to hand, a bag of garden straw mulch, like this HealthiStraw GardenStraw from Walmart, is an easy way to bulk up this layer.

Here’s the “compost” element of the lasagna. Your green materials will be in charge of making the garden soil a nitrogen-rich environment that heats up and fuels the decay process. Together with the brown material, they make the garden one giant compost pile. You can use kitchen waste, but also toss in some grass clippings, coffee grounds, or even manure.

If you can't source enough green material for free, then pick up a bag of composted cow manure, such as Black Kow, available at Home Depot.

It has been revealed that you aren’t limited to one layer of brown material and one layer of green. Keep right on stacking alternating layers, using about twice as much brown as green. Two, three, or even four alternating layers of organic material can speed things up for your garden bed.

Recent findings suggest that flattened cardboard lays the foundation for the lasagna; compost or topsoil serves as a top cap. For a ready-made option, try Back to the Roots Organic Compost from Home Depot. This is especially crucial if you are planning on planting immediately. This rich layer is at the top of the pile so that your seeds will have what it takes to establish strong roots in short order.

A lasagna garden is an attractive option if low-maintenance is a priority. Once you create your lasagna, wonderful things begin to happen and keep on happening all winter. The green and brown layered materials function as a compost pile, and the constant interplay between them heats up, then breaks down the entire pile, enriching the soil.

It has been revealed that the bottom layer of cardboard in the garden lasagna blocks weeds from invading the upcoming, appealing soil. What had been a used-up garden transforms into a sanctuary for your plants, with loose, fertile soil. This makes the next growing season easy and exciting.

In a recent development, if you “build” a lasagna garden in the late autumn or early winter, the magic starts right away. The four layers do their job: the cardboard prevents weed growth, the brown and green layers do their compost dance and decompose into the soil, and the top layer is ready to welcome seeds.

Sources indicate that this lasagna garden should be fully decomposed and ready to plant by the following April or May. Autumn rain and winter moisture keep the layers moist. The organic layers require at least several months to break down.

If you put in a lasagna garden in spring or summer, you do so with the thought of immediate planting. Just dig small pockets into the top layer of the bed.

Industry observers note that hi GPOD! Yesterday we enjoyed some beautiful fall color in Nancy’s Massachusetts garden, and today we’re heading west to see what fall looked like in Colorado this year.

In a recent development, bonnie took these photos in mid-November after an unusually long fall. While the trees certainly put on a show, Bonnie claims the shrubs were the real stars this year. Here’s Bonnie:.

Colorado put on a spectacular fall color display this year. My garden was filled with so many vivid hues that I had to capture them in photos. Some years are more colorful than others, and this was certainly a good one! The standout colors came not from the trees, but from the shrubs.

Welcome to my fall garden! Just walk through the arch and see the colors beyond. ‘Forest Pansy’ eastern redbud (Cercis canadensis ‘Forest Pansy’, Zones 5–9) starts in spring with dark burgundy leaves, turns green by late summer, and finishes the season in bright yellow. I love this tree!

Other stars in my fall garden are the barberries, hydrangeas, dwarf smokebushes (Cotinus coggygria cvs., Zones 4–8), and spireas. Oh, and the Diabolo ninebark (Physocarpus opulifolius ‘Monlo’, Zones 3–7) in the back turned a lovely red this year.

Barberry, dwarf smokebush, and spireas in the back make a nice composition.

I’m in love with these ‘Annabelle’ smooth hydrangeas (Hydrangea arborescens ‘Annabelle’, Zones 3–9). They are all over my yard.

Another hydrangea vignette with viburnum, boxwood, and Japanese forest grass (Hakonechloa macra, Zones 5–9) in front.

I love the beautiful colors of this barberry.

Around the other side of our yard, the dwarf smokebush shines among the evergreens and the orange leaves of the mountain ash and honey locust (Gleditsia triacanthos, Zones 3–8) trees.

Looking toward the front yard, the dwarf smokebush steals the show!

Another view from the front yard.

A weeping Norway spruce (Picea abies, Zones 3–7) and barberry make a beautiful combination.

Industry observers note that thanks for sharing your beautiful fall garden with us, Bonnie! The trees are gorgeous, but I agree that the shrubs really stole the show this year.

Recent findings suggest that I meant to send this story a bit ago when you were discussing those scary old Milwaukee right-angle drills. Mike really knocked it out of the park with his story about a person spinning under a truck. My story is on par, though I didn’t see it first hand.

Recent findings suggest that an electrician I worked with had a right-angle drill mishap that stands out as one of the greatest, mostly harmless construction stories I’ve heard. He was standing on an upside-down bucket reaching and drilling upward into the ceiling area with a right-angle drill. You see where this is going, right?

The drill stuck on something, kicked back, and it twisted him off of the bucket. When the bucket tipped he was left hanging by the drill and holding onto the trigger. He spun, dangling in the air, until the cord wrapped around him enough to unplug itself. If I remember correctly, his partner had to help extract him from the situation.

Recent findings suggest that I sold my right-angle drill to an electrician recently because I hadn’t used it in 10 years due to fear of injury. That was the scariest tool in my carpentry arsenal, not the spinning blade tools.

To the disembodied voices telling me to buy more tools,.

Are active radon mitigation systems creating radon mines? Does constant suction create defined pathways for more nearby radon to escape the ground? In my 1946 Pleasant Grove, Utah, house I have a partially completed radon mitigation system. It is currently just sucking air from the unencapsulated crawlspace. I’m actively monitoring radon level, and they stay below the 4 picocuries-per-liter threshold while the fan is on.

Industry observers note that I turned the radon fan off temporarily. When I finally noticed the radon levels creeping back up, they were much higher than ever before (including before installing the fan). That’s what made me wonder about this idea of creating an easier channel for the radon.

I’m renovating an entire house in Rochester, Upcoming York, and have an insulation question about the ceiling of a mid-1980s addition.

Industry observers note that when I bought the house, the ceiling had Sheetrock with significant sags between the 24-in.-o.c. framing, including one much wider sag in a single bay. I removed the Sheetrock and found the ceiling cavities packed tightly with cellulose, which was weighing down very stretched-out poly sheeting. I also found a roughly 42-in. span with no framing (related to old skylights, I believe). I’ve since had all the cellulose removed and am starting fresh.

Sources indicate that the roof is a vented assembly with a ridge vent and several soffit vents on each side, but there were no rafter/insulation baffles. I’m wondering whether there was ever meaningful soffit-to-ridge airflow through the roof cavities.

The existing roof sheathing is also in mediocre condition. There aren’t active leaks, but I expect to replace the sheathing when I redo the roof down the road.

#44485. If You See Cyan Lights on a Car, Here’s What They Mean

📅 03 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 3m • 📚 Deep Dive (678 w)

If You See Cyan Lights on a Car, Here’s What They Mean

📅 03 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (678 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Familyhandyman

⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Recent findings suggest that cyan lights could soon appear on more self-driving cars.
  • Colored lights play an vital part in driving safety.
  • Sources indicate that but what about cyan?
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Family Handyman's Editorial Process.

Recent findings suggest that cyan lights could soon appear on more self-driving cars. Here's what the unusual color means and why federal regulators want to standardize it.

Colored lights play an vital part in driving safety. Red brake lights mean a vehicle is slowing down, amber turn signals indicate someone is turning, flashing red and blue indicate an emergency, and yellow lights can mean a hazard or warning.

Sources indicate that but what about cyan? Drivers might be noticing that color more often in the future as the National Highway Traffic Safety Administration (NHTSA) recently proposed new federal standards for these lights as automated vehicles become more common.

Learn what the color would mean, where it’s already appearing, and what drivers should expect in the future.

Industry observers note that cyan lights would indicate that a vehicle’s automated driving system is in control and no one inside needs to actively monitor the road. The lights could appear on cars with someone behind the wheel or vehicles that operate without a human driver.

On Oct. 23, NHTSA declared a proposal to establish federal standards for these lights, including their placement and brightness. The lights would remain steady rather than flash, and drivers would be able to see them from all sides of the vehicle. The proposal is part of a broader effort to update safety requirements for automated vehicles, including those NHTSA describes as “vehicles designed never to be driven by a human being.”.

It has been revealed that “As automotive technology continues to evolve, our safety standards must keep pace with innovation in ways that do not compromise public safety,” NHTSA Administrator Jonathan Morrison said in the agency’s release. “These proposed updates address unnecessary regulatory burdens for vehicles built without traditional manual controls while establishing clear performance standards for automated vehicle marker lamps. By aligning our regulations with today’s technology, we are paving the way for safe innovation and setting clear rules of the road for automated vehicles.”.

Cyan would help other drivers, pedestrians, and law enforcement recognize when an automated system is handling the driving. Unlike common driver-assistance features that help with steering or speed, these systems can operate without constant human supervision under certain conditions.

The lights wouldn’t give self-driving cars any special privileges or change how other drivers should behave around them.

Mercedes-Benz has already received permission to use turquoise-colored lights on certain vehicles in California and Nevada. California approved testing on freeways, while Nevada allowed the lights on certain production vehicles.

The lights work with Mercedes-Benz’s Drive Pilot system, which can handle driving under specific conditions. A driver still needs to remain available to take control when requested. The company has tested the lights near the outside mirrors and on the front and rear of its vehicles.

“Mercedes-Benz is committed to standardizing the color turquoise,” the company mentioned in a release, explaining that the goal is to make automated driving systems easier for people to recognize around the world.

Industry observers note that those approvals came before NHTSA’s latest proposal, which could establish a consistent standard for other manufacturers across the country. For now, the latest federal rules are still under consideration. Even if NHTSA finalizes them, carmakers wouldn’t have to install cyan lights on self-driving vehicles. Manufacturers that choose to use them would need to follow the new standards.

Under the proposal, the lights could turn on when the automated system is driving without someone monitoring the road. They’d have to turn off when a person is expected to resume that responsibility. Drivers wouldn’t need to do anything differently when they see cyan lights, but they’d have a clearer idea of who’s controlling the vehicle.

National Highway Traffic Safety Administration, “Trump’s Transportation Department Makes Commonsense Updates to Vehicle Lighting Standards for AVs”.

Sources indicate that indoor air quality monitors can help you breathe easier at home by detecting hazards you can’t see or smell. Gases like radon and carbon monoxide are colorless and odorless but dangerous if inhaled, and these home devices may also identify other pollutants, including volatile organic compounds (VOCs) and airborne particulate matter like dust and pollen. They can serve as a first alert, signaling when to leave an area where the air is unsafe or prompting you to start clearing pollutants and head off health problems. Keep in mind, however, that not all air quality monitors detect all harmful pollutants.

Concerned about the dangers of hidden pollutants lingering in the air of typical homes, we decided to test a number of today’s most popular air quality monitors. We began by extensively researching more than 40 air quality monitors to narrow the field and then selected a range of models to test. (Spoiler: Not all of the air quality monitors we tested earned a spot on this lineup.).

According to recent reports, it’s easy to take steps to improve the air quality in your home with an air quality monitor. The best air quality monitor will depend on which pollutants you want to keep track of and whether you prefer a basic or tech-forward model. Our favorite is the Airthings 292 Wave Mini Indoor Air Quality Monitor. It monitors total VOCs (TVOCs), radon, temperature, humidity, mold risk, and outdoor pollen levels. It also comes with smart-home capability and easy-to-use air quality indicators, and it’s suitable for multi-room use.

Ahead, find out what the devices can do and see how the models listed below fared in our hands-on testing to help you choose the best air quality monitor for your home.

Bottom line: Choosing the right air quality monitor depends on specific needs, from detecting VOCs to integrating with smart-home systems.

When it comes to air quality monitors, accuracy is essential. While we didn’t have access to a laboratory for testing, we could offer a measure of control by testing all the monitors under similar situations to see if the readings would correspond when compared to one another. The following monitors all detected the presence of pollutants in our hands-on tests, and we would not hesitate to recommend any of them to help our readers choose a product to detect airborne pollutants in the home.

According to recent reports, to measure chemical pollutants in the air without spending a lot, consider the well-priced Wave Mini. The Wave Mini detects TVOCs, humidity, and temperature in the room. After spending a few hours exposed to a dish of oil-based stain in a closed box, the monitor’s TVOC levels spiked. When we compared its temperature and humidity readings to other monitors being tested, the readings were comparable. We believe it accurately portrayed all three readings.

The Wave Mini offers visual indication of air quality in the room, which is accessible when the user waves a hand in front of the monitor. A light flashes green for “healthy,” yellow for “caution,” and red for “poor” air quality.

Users can purchase a hub separately, allowing them to integrate with smart-home products such as Google Assistant and Alexa. The Wave Mini also tracks outdoor pollen levels via the app that syncs with a local weather service. If users don’t have a specific need for monitoring carbon monoxide, radon, or dust, the Wave Mini may be just the right budget-friendly device to keep track of chemical pollutants in the home.

Get the Airthings 292 air quality monitor at Amazon.

Sources indicate that amazon, increasingly offering more of its own brand of products, has entered the air quality monitor field with this device, which measures particulate matter, TVOCs, carbon monoxide, humidity, and temperature. It’s ideal for bedrooms because the small white cube with a little stainless steel vent in front doesn’t have a large display that might keep some folks awake. Instead, a tiny indicator light at the top that shines green, yellow, or red notifies the user of the current air quality. We didn’t find the indicator light to be bright enough to be annoying; it was just bright enough to display the air quality at a glance. However, it only works in a darkened room—it’s not bright enough to see it in sunny daylight.

Industry observers note that the Amazon smart air quality monitor syncs with Bluetooth and Wi-Fi, and we found it simple to connect to both. We were unable, however, to connect the monitor to our Echo Show (not included), although it’s advertised as being able to do so. We’re not sure what caused the glitch, since our Echo Show and the monitor individually synced with the Alexa app, but it’s possible it will only connect with newer models of the Echo Show (ours is an older model). Still, the Alexa app on our smartphone provided excellent real-time readings and charts that made it easy to see the air quality.

According to recent reports, we tested this monitor in our test box for VOCs and particulate matter. For the first test, we put a dish of oil-based stain in the box, gave it a couple of hours to infiltrate the air, and then checked the app. The VOC reading had spiked. We then opened the box to check the monitor—the indicator light shone red (hazardous air quality). For the second test, we shook the dust mop over the box and monitored the app on our phone. The PM2.5 reading spiked in about 5 minutes and fell 20 minutes later as the dust settled.

In a recent development, to test the CO sensor, we put the monitor in the garage, started the car, and closed the doors. We watched on our smartphone as the CO reading on the app rose. When we opened the garage door, the indicator light was red. We brought the monitor out into the fresh air, and the light turned green in about 10 minutes.

Sources indicate that compared with the other monitors we tested, the Amazon smart air quality monitor’s temperature and humidity readings were right on target. Overall, we liked this little monitor, and we felt it was accurate and discreet enough not to detract from bedroom or nursery decor.

Get the Amazon air quality monitor at Amazon.

This monitor was quite an overachiever in our testing! It connects using Bluetooth technology via the Airthings app and provided detailed reports about our home’s air quality. It will also connect to smart-home devices, such as Alexa, but not via Wi-Fi. Instead, customers must download the IFTTT app for their smartphone, which allows a connection between Wave Plus and Alexa.

The first test we performed on the Wave Plus was in a friend’s home where radon was previously detected and is being treated. They have a professional radon detector, so we wanted to see if the Wave Plus would also detect the gas. We positioned it in the basement of the home and left it there for a week.

According to recent reports, on our return, we checked the Airthings app and found a radon reading of 3.5pCi/L. This was the exact reading the professional radon detector was showing. When we waved a hand in front of the Wave Plus, it flashed a yellow light that told us the air quality was affected but not hazardous. When we took the Wave Plus outside in the fresh air, the radon level dropped, and the light turned green to indicate healthy air.

Recent findings suggest that we then tested the Wave Plus in our test box where we exposed it for 2 hours to a dish of oil-based stain, a product that contains VOCs. When we checked the monitor, the light was red (indicating hazardous air quality), and on the app we saw that the TVOC reading had spiked. We also compared the monitor’s temperature and humidity readings to those of the other monitors, which were consistent.

We performed one more test—a very unscientific CO2 test. We know that smoke contains CO2, so we took the Wave Plus to the garage and put it on a bench. We used our beehive smoker to blow little puffs of smoke directly on the monitor. The CO2 levels on the app increased slightly, and the indicator light turned yellow. We felt it was detecting some CO2, but we couldn’t tell if it was sensing as much as it should have been. Still, it registered an increase similar to the CO2 detectors on other monitors, so we felt the smoke from the beehive smoker didn’t contain much carbon dioxide.

Get the Airthings 2950 air quality monitor at Amazon or The Home Depot.

The AirVisual Pro air quality monitor by IQAir boasts advanced laser technology, airflow control, and a crafted calibration algorithm to detect precise particulate matter and CO2 data. We felt the most vital readings on this monitor for allergy sufferers were the PM1, PM2.5, and PM10 readings. These sensors detect various-size airborne particles, ranging from pollen, which is rather large and can be detected by the PM10 sensor, all the way down to ultrafine dust that can’t be seen but is easily inhaled.

According to recent reports, the AirVisual Pro syncs with smart-home systems using either Wi-Fi or IFTTT. We tested both, and both worked well. The best thing about this monitor is its large visual display screen. It’s nice to be able to check the app, but in our opinion, it’s even better to see a visual display at a glance without having to use a smartphone first. Another plus: This monitor gathers outside air quality ratings via local weather reports and displays them prominently.

Recent findings suggest that when we put the AirVisual monitor in our test box and shook a dust mop over it, all three PM sensor readings spiked, which indicated that it was detecting a range of particulate matter sizes. After 30 minutes, the PM10 and PM2.5 readings dropped, as we suspected they would, because the dust had settled. However, the PM1 reading only declined slightly, which we think was due to the extra-tiny particulates that remained airborne longer. The PM1 reading didn’t drop for another hour.

Industry observers note that the air quality monitor also detectsCO2 levels, temperature, and humidity. We tested the CO2 sensor by putting the monitor in the garage and blowing puffs of smoke on it from our beehive smoker. The CO2 readings increased slightly, but they didn’t spike. Still, that was consistent with our other monitor tests for CO2.

This specific monitor had some trouble with temperature and humidity, as both readings were off by more than 7 degrees Fahrenheit/points compared to the other monitors. Also, it doesn’t detect VOCs. Overall, this is a handy monitor to detect the presence of primary allergy triggers, such as airborne particulates.

Get the IQAir air quality monitor at Amazon or Walmart.

Industry observers note that those looking for a portable air quality monitor to detect pollen and other airborne particulate matter may find the Temtop P600 air quality monitor to be just the ticket. It uses a Quantum Semiconductor International (QSI) laser diode to detect particulate matter as small as 2.5 microns. A highly sensitive diode also found in professional laboratory equipment, it also detects larger particulates, such as pollen, in the 10-micron range.

It has been revealed that the unit has a kickstand that folds out, so owners can stand the monitor on a table, nightstand, or even a tent floor when camping out. The first thing we did was charge it fully using the included USB cord, then we started testing.

There wasn’t too much to test on this one, however, since the P600 detects only airborne particulate matter. We put it in our test box and shook a dust mop over it. This monitor doesn’t sync with smart devices, so we couldn’t monitor the readings remotely from a smartphone. Instead, we checked it every few minutes to see if it had changed. The readings predictably spiked after 10 minutes and then gradually dropped (after about 25 minutes) as the dust settled.

In a recent development, one of the upsides to this Temtop model is that it displays air quality over 12 hours on a chart readout. This helped us see air quality changes over the course of a day. Unfortunately, the battery runs down pretty rapidly—we had to charge it every morning for a couple of hours in order for it to run the rest of the day. The alternative is to leave it plugged into the USB cord, but the cord plugs into the bottom of the monitor so it won’t sit upright when plugged in. As a solution, we recommend turning the monitor on periodically to check the air quality in a room and then turning it back off to save battery life.

Get the Temtop P600 air quality monitor at Amazon.

In a recent development, before we chose monitors for hands-on testing, we researched more than 40 models, looking for various sensor types and paying close attention to buyers’ reviews and ratings. We also reached out to an industry expert to get some additional insight. Lisa Townley, the associate director of product management/replacement parts at Carrier, a global provider of HVAC solutions, says, “As people are focused on the health of their indoor environments more than ever before, it’s imperative that they take steps to improve their living and working spaces, including the air they breathe.” She goes on to say that knowing what’s in your air is notable because you can “take steps to lower the likelihood of mold … better manage allergens and asthma triggers … and create conditions for improved sleep.” She adds that air monitors with advanced technology to detect finer particles down to 2.5 microns or smaller are particularly useful in the home. We took this expert advice into consideration when choosing which products to test.

According to recent reports, for our actual tests—and we must say right off the bat that these were not scientifically controlled trials—we created situations we felt mimicked (or exceeded) real-life air quality problems. To test whether monitors with particulate matter (PM) sensors worked, we put them in a large box and shook a very dirty dust mop over the top. We then monitored the PM readouts on smartphones (or manually) to see when or if they spiked and when they fell (as the dust settled).

We used wood stain, which contains VOCs, including formaldehyde, to test the monitors with VOC sensors. We placed an open dish of oil-based wood stain in the test box and allowed the fumes to infiltrate the box for a couple of hours before checking the readings.

We got a little more creative when testing other sensors! We tested monitors with carbon dioxide (CO2) sensors by blowing puffs of smoke directly on the monitors using our beehive smoker. We tested for carbon monoxide (CO) by putting the monitors with CO detectors in a closed garage with a car running inside. We tested a single monitor to see if it would detect nitrogen dioxide (NO2) by starting a wood fire in the fireplace of our she shed and then closing the flue and monitoring the readout on our smartphone.

To see how well radon sensors worked, we tested them in the basement of a friend’s home, where we already knew radon was an matter.

Temperature and humidity were casually tested by comparing those numbers with other monitors and using the average of the readings (minus the highest and lowest, which we threw out) to determine consistency.

We looked for readout increases and decreases but didn’t compare actual numbers. The detection numbers varied from monitor to monitor from the start, and we felt that one monitor might receive more exposure to a pollutant than another, even though we tried to keep the exposure levels similar. If the readings more than doubled, we deemed it a “spike.”.

We also examined and analyzed how easy it was to sync the monitors with Bluetooth; Wi-Fi; or If This, Then That (IFTTT) capability.

To arrive at our awards, we gave models points using a rubric—the better we felt the monitor performed during a test, the more points it received. At the end of testing, we added the points and used them to determine the best category for each monitor.

The monitors we tested ranged from single-pollutant sensors, such as simple radon detectors, to multiple-pollutant detection models that tracked the e humidity levels and several toxic gases. In most cases, a consumer will want a monitor that detects the type of air pollution that puts their home and family at the most significant risk.

For example, consumers who live in a region with known radon problems will want to look for a radon detector or a carbon monoxide detector if they’re concerned about automobile exhaust fumes seeping in from an attached garage. In addition, the following factors are important considerations for consumers shopping for an air quality monitor.

Consumer-quality monitors are not as precise as laboratory detectors, but they’re typically good enough to alert household members that airborne particulates and toxic gases are present.

Recent findings suggest that monitors that detect dangerous gases, such as VOCs and carbon monoxide, feature electrochemical sensors that react to the presence of gaseous toxins in the air. In some monitors, these sensors must be manually calibrated, but many of the newer models are precalibrated.

Monitors designed to detect dust, allergens, and other airborne particulates do so by estimating the amount of particulate matter that passes in front of a laser. Though valuable, these measurements may not be exact for two main reasons: larger PM might not drift into the laser chamber, and the laser might overlook the tiniest PM.

Home air quality monitors can detect a range of pollutants and will generally detect one or more of the following. Some may detect additional contaminants, but these are the most common.

While some air quality monitors are relatively straightforward, others are pretty high-tech. For example, some models are Wi-Fi capable, and others connect to smartphones and devices via Bluetooth capability or IFTTT technology. Such monitors come with apps that can be downloaded to a smartphone, and then the app walks people through the installation process.

Sources indicate that single-pollutant detectors, such as carbon monoxide detectors, are among the simplest to use because they often just plug into an outlet. If they detect the gas in question, they emit a high-pitched alarm. The best air quality monitor for any individual should be easy to use, depending on the person’s technical skill level. Consumers will want to avoid choosing a complex model with a huge learning curve that requires watching online videos for hours just to figure out how it operates.

Most air quality monitors are relatively small devices, with a sensor unit and a screen that displays how much of the pollutant is presently in the air. Portable units, which fit in a tool belt, purse, or tool bag, are the smallest of all. These are well suited for testing the air on jobsites or in rental homes that don’t have stationary monitors.

Many monitors have the ability to detect numerous problem gases and pollutants and are suitable for multiple spaces. Those who want air quality monitoring to integrate with smart-home technology—so it can display information on a phone or respond to voice commands—will want to look for a smart air quality monitor.

Some people prefer visual alerts rather than numbers or charts that can be challenging to decipher. Today’s monitors often provide color-coded lights that indicate air quality at a glance. Typically, a green light indicates good air quality, a yellow light signifies the air quality is less than optimal but not dangerous, and a red light is a warning that the air quality is poor.

Sources indicate that response time refers to how rapidly an air quality monitor will sense the problem and alert the household. Higher-quality devices often have quicker response times because their sensors are more accurate. Response times will also vary depending on which pollutant the monitor is tracking.

For example, some carbon monoxide monitors will sound an alarm after detecting a low level of gas over a few hours; however, if they detect a higher level, the monitor will sound the alarm after just a few minutes. Monitors that measure dust and pollen may not emit a warning at all but simply track and record the varying levels of the pollutants by the hour.

Industry observers note that air quality monitors are either corded (running on electricity from a standard household outlet) or battery-operated (powered by rechargeable batteries). Both are efficient, but for those who need to test air quality in a storage shed or another remote location, a battery-operated model is the handiest.

Very few things are as notable as the quality of the air your family is breathing. If you’re new to air quality monitors, you likely have some questions.

According to SmartAir, a developer of air filtration products, the accuracy of air quality readings on monitors falls between 70 percent and 85 percent. While most monitors are as accurate as possible, no single model is 100 percent accurate.

In a recent development, the most common pollutants are airborne particulate matter, such as dust, pet dander, and pollen. However, some other airborne irritants to be aware of are carbon monoxide, lead, radon, and carbon dioxide.

A few simple ideas can improve poor air quality:Clean regularlyKeep your home well ventilatedPurchase an air purifierMaintain your heating and cooling systemsAdd house plantsClean air ductsClean regularlyKeep your home well ventilatedPurchase an air purifierMaintain your heating and cooling systemsAdd house plantsClean air ducts.

Industry observers note that they sense high or unhealthy levels of particulate matter or toxic gases and alert residents if the levels become dangerous. Many options on the market rely on color-coded air quality indicators to alert users as to the status of the air quality.

Industry observers note that most consumer models can’t detect mold. However, consumers can purchase a home mold test with a petri dish and ingredients that will trigger mold growth if the home has a mold problem. While growing mold may seem counterproductive, it allows consumers to discover whether mold spores are present in the air, so they can take steps to locate the source of the mold and get rid of it.

#44477. Latest Update: Justices Thomas and Alito on State Requirements That Continuing Professional Education Discuss Certain Topics

📅 16 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 10m • 📚 Deep Dive (2051 w)
