Latest Update: Justices Thomas and Alito on State Requirements That Continuing Professional Education Discuss Certain Topics

📅 16 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 10 min read (2051 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Reason

⏱️ ~10 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • From Justice Thomas's dissent from denial of certiorari today in Khatibi v.
  • In 2022, California began requiring private instructors in privately run and privately accredited continuing medical education (CME) courses to discuss how so-called implicit bias affects healthcare outcomes.
  • I would have granted certiorari to clarify the government-speech doctrine.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

From Justice Thomas's dissent from denial of certiorari today in Khatibi v. Yip, joined by Justice Alito (Justice Gorsuch voted to grant the petition, but didn't sign on to the dissent):.

In 2022, California began requiring private instructors in privately run and privately accredited continuing medical education (CME) courses to discuss how so-called implicit bias affects healthcare outcomes. The Ninth Circuit held that First Amendment scrutiny did not apply to this compelled-speech requirement because the breadth of California's CME regulation renders the content of any CME course government speech, not private speech. That logic fundamentally misunderstands this Court's precedents and the Constitution. First Amendment protections do not give way simply because a State heavily regulates speech.

I would have granted certiorari to clarify the government-speech doctrine. At a minimum, the Ninth Circuit misapplied Shurtleff v. Boston (2022), which instructs courts to identify government speech by considering (1) "the history of the expression at glitch," (2) "the public's likely perception as to who (the government or a private person) is speaking," and (3) "the extent to which the government has actively shaped or controlled the expression." The Ninth Circuit collapsed those distinct inquiries, focusing on the breadth of the government's regulatory scheme at each step. More fundamentally, however, Shurtleff is leading courts astray.

I joined Justice ALITO's concurrence in Shurtleff, which warned that the majority's three-factor test could cause courts to conclude that extensive government regulation transforms a private message into government speech exempt from First Amendment scrutiny. As the Ninth Circuit's decision shows, those concerns were prescient. This Court should reconsider whether the Shurtleff test is the proper mode of analysis for identifying government speech….

According to recent reports, california-licensed physicians are required to complete 50 hours of approved CME every two years. Credit-eligible CME courses are often organized by private entities, certified by private accreditors, and taught by private instructors. The State does not preapprove course content but reserves the right to audit courses for compliance with its CME standards.

Sources indicate that the Medical Board of California "adopt[s] and administer[s] [CME] standards," few of which relate to course content. In addition, the State requires that CME courses broadly relate to the medical profession. They must "serve to maintain, develop, or increase the knowledge, skills, and professional performance that a physician and surgeon uses to provide care, or to improve the quality of care provided to patients." In 2019, however, the California Legislature added a requirement that after January 1, 2022, all CME courses must "contain curriculum that includes the understanding of implicit bias." To satisfy that requirement, CME courses must contain "[e]xamples of how implicit bias affects perceptions and treatment decisions of physicians and surgeons, leading to disparities in health outcomes" or "[s]trategies to address how unintended biases in decisionmaking may contribute to health care disparities.".

Petitioners Dr. Azadeh Khatibi and Do No Harm do not want to speak California's preferred message on implicit bias, and they challenged § 2190.1(d) as compelling speech in violation of the First Amendment. Dr. Khatibi, a California-licensed ophthalmologist, creates and teaches CME courses. She "disagrees that implicit bias is the primary factor driving disparities in healthcare" and does not want to devote time to the subject during her courses. Do No Harm is a nonprofit corporation. At least one of its members teaches CME courses and believes that implicit bias trainings "have not been shown to successfully reduce barriers to healthcare, and instead risk infecting healthcare decisions with divisive and discriminatory ideas." Yet, California's implicit-bias-training requirement leaves petitioners no choice but to discuss the topic in a way that affirms the State's view that implicit bias causes "disparities in health outcomes…..

It has been revealed that the Ninth Circuit held that all three Shurtleff factors indicate that "CMEs eligible for Board credit constitute government speech." At every step of the analysis, the Ninth Circuit emphasized the breadth of the State's regulation. Considering history, the court noted that California "has long regulated the practice of medicine as an exercise of the police power" and has "adopted, updated, and enforced CME standards." Considering the public's likely perception of the speaker in a CME course, the court reasoned that "licensees could attribute approved CMEs' content to California" because "their profession is heavily regulated." Considering the extent to which the government has shaped the expression, the court cited "California's extraordinary control over accredited CMEs." As Judge VanDyke explained in his dissent from the denial of rehearing en banc, the panel's "approach boil[ed] down to a single-factor analysis: does the government 'heavily' or 'actively' regulate CMEs?" ….

In its blinkered application of the Shurtleff factors, the Ninth Circuit lost sight of the core government-speech inquiry: whether the government is "speak[ing] for itself or … regulat[ing] private expression.".

Industry observers note that the government-speech doctrine occupies a narrow corner of our First Amendment jurisprudence. The First Amendment protects the people's right of free speech against government interference; it does not prevent the government from speaking for itself. "But courts must be very careful when a government claims that speech by one or more private speakers is actually government speech." "If private speech could be passed off as government speech by simply affixing a government seal of approval, government could … muffle the expression of disfavored viewpoints," or, as here, require private speakers to convey government messages without facing any constitutional scrutiny.

This Court has thus exercised "great caution" before characterizing a message as government speech. In Johanns v. Livestock Marketing Assn (2005), we held that government-sponsored beef ads constituted government speech because the government determined "the overarching message" of the ads, helped develop proposals for the ads, reviewed every ad "for substance and for wording," and the Secretary of Agriculture "exercise[d] final approval authority over every word used in every" ad. In Pleasant Grove City v. Summum (2009), we held that the permanent display of monuments in a public park was government speech because the City "effectively controlled the messages sent by the monuments in the Park by exercising final approval authority over their selection." And, in Walker v. Texas Div., Sons of Confederate Veterans, Inc. (2015), we held that the messages on government-issued license plates, over which the State "maintain[ed] direct control," were government speech.

Since Walker—which we have described as the "outer boun[d] of the government-speech doctrine," Matal v. Tam (2017)—we have been careful to distinguish between government control over messages and government control over the broader scheme through which the messages are communicated. We held, for example, that trademarks are private speech, notwithstanding the government's substantial involvement in the registration process. And, this Court held that flags flown outside of Boston's City Hall did not constitute government speech in part because the city regularly permitted private groups to freely fly their own colors. In all these cases, the controlling question was whether "the government intends to speak for itself or to regulate private expression.".

Put in those simple terms, and in light of our precedents, California's attempt to require private individuals in privately accredited CME courses to run implicit-bias training is an evident attempt "to regulate private expression." … First, California has not historically used CME to communicate government messages. While the State requires that CME courses generally relate to the practice of medicine and occasionally requires that courses cover certain subjects, California has not otherwise dictated the content of courses.

Second, because California "relie[s] on the participation of private parties in executing the CME scheme," the public is unlikely to perceive a private instructor's CME course as government speech. As the Ninth Circuit acknowledged, Dr. Khatibi "plausibly alleged facts suggesting that attendees treat her as the person responsible for CME content.".

According to recent reports, third, while California extensively regulates the medical field, licenses physicians, and sets the requirements for credit-eligible CME, there is little evidence that California "shape[s] the messages" communicated in CME courses. Despite its long recitation of California regulations, the Ninth Circuit did not identify any state law that requires private speakers in a CME course to express a particular viewpoint—even on contestable medical concerns. The implicit-bias-training requirement is a notable departure from that practice. It should have been easy, then, for the courts below to conclude that California's implicit-bias-training requirement regulates private speech.

More troubling than the Ninth Circuit's misapplication of the Shurtleff factors are the implications of the court's decision. On the Ninth Circuit's view of government speech, could California require a CME instructor to communicate the State's preferred message on the availability of abortion? Could the State require a CME instructor to inform participants that for certain patients, gender-transition surgery is ethically required?

Recent findings suggest that what of other professions whose members California licenses and regulates? At the next statewide legal conference at which lectures are offered for continuing legal education, could California require a keynote speaker to oppose racial preferences in law firm hiring? Applying the Ninth Circuit's logic, enough government regulation of the field would convert the private speaker's message in each of these hypotheticals into government speech unprotected by the First Amendment. That result does not follow from this Court's precedents, and it certainly does not follow from the Constitution….

Sources indicate that if the Ninth Circuit's decision is truly the kind of result that Shurtleff's three-factor test countenances, we should reconsider Shurtleff. Before Shurtleff, this Court had identified history, public perception, and government control as "relevant" but not mandatory "considerations" for identifying government speech. When Shurtleff described those considerations as a three-factor test, several Members of the Court—myself included—warned that the test would be unworkable and obscure the central inquiry in government-speech cases: whether the government is speaking or regulating private speech. "[L]ike any factorized analysis," the Shurtleff majority's approach does not "provide a principled way of deciding cases." Worse, myopic focus on the history and scope of government control over speech may give courts the false impression that state regulation can convert private speech into government speech.

After only a few years, those concerns are materializing. The Ninth Circuit relied on California's regulation of CME to conclude that requiring private speakers to communicate a government message was not compelled speech but government speech. That is precisely the paradox predicted by the concurrence in Shurtleff: that "government action that regulates private speech would" now "qualify as government speech unregulated by the First Amendment." But, neither compelled speech nor "[c]ensorship" are "made constitutional by aggressive and direct application." It cannot be the case that compelled speech becomes government speech because the government has compelled the speech.

Industry observers note that I would grant certiorari to correct course. In my view, the relevant inquiry in a government-speech case is straightforward: Is the government "speaking," or is it "regulating private expression"? The challenged government activity must be "government speech in the literal sense—purposeful communication of a governmentally determined message by a person acting within the scope of a power to speak for the government." Moreover, "the government must … not rely on a means that abridges the speech of persons acting in a private capacity," because doing so reveals that the government has moved from the role of speaker to that of regulator.

According to recent reports, under this framework, it is easy to see why California's law is subject to First Amendment scrutiny. The State's implicit-bias-training requirement is not speech by any government actor; it is a requirement that private speakers communicate certain messages. Although the government may "deputiz[e] private persons as its agents" to convey its message, Dr. Khatibi and Do No Harm's members have not "voluntarily assumed" "a public or quasi-public capacity that empowers them to speak on behalf of the government." They share their own messages through the CME courses they create and deliver, and they do so in their private capacities. Even "government speech in the literal sense is not exempt from First Amendment attack if it uses a means that restricts private expression," such as "compelled speech." When, as here, the government does not issue its own messages but instead requires private speakers to communicate the government's viewpoint, the First Amendment applies….

Sources indicate that A State cannot regulate its way out of First Amendment scrutiny. We should not permit the government-speech doctrine to be wielded as "a cover for censorship" or a cloak for compelled speech.

Sources indicate that A short level works for some projects, but longer surfaces need a wider check. Learn how to pick the right size and use it accurately.

Levels come in many different shapes and sizes, and figuring out how long a level should be for a certain project isn’t always straightforward. Choosing the right size matters because a level that’s too short can miss uneven spots, while one that’s too long can be difficult to use in tight spaces.

Here’s how much of a surface a level should cover, which sizes work best, and when overhang is okay.

In a recent development, it depends on the project, but a longer level is usually better for checking bigger surfaces. A shorter one might show that the middle of a board is level without catching a problem closer to either end.

The level doesn’t have to stretch across the entire surface, though. A 24-inch level can work on a four-foot shelf, for example, as long as the installer checks several spots along its length. For longer surfaces, a smaller level can sit on a long, straight board to check a wider area. A laser level is another option, especially when lining up things across a room.

The way the level sits on the material matters, too. A little sawdust or dirt underneath can affect the reading, so both surfaces should be clean. The tool also needs to sit firmly without rocking.

There’s no set rule for how much of a surface a level needs to cover, but it should fit comfortably and have enough contact to stay steady.

Different sizes work better for different jobs:.

According to recent reports, “Use a 4-foot carpenter’s level for framing whenever you have room for its length,” according to The Home Depot. “Warps or waves in the boards can throw off a shorter carpenter’s level.”.

According to recent reports, another common concern is whether the level can hang over the edge of whatever is being checked. Some overhang is fine, provided the tool has enough support to stay steady.

If it starts tipping or rocking, a shorter level will likely work better. The bubble doesn’t need to be directly above the material, either. It can still give an accurate reading even when that part of the tool hangs past the edge.

According to recent reports, A clean, properly maintained fireplace is more likely to operate as designed. On the other hand, excessive buildup, restricted airflow, and neglected components can interfere with ignition, combustion, and draft.

  • Maryland is one of several States that prohibit law-abiding gun owners from carrying firearms in a wide variety of public places.
  • According to recent reports, I am skeptical that each of these laws "is consistent with this Nation's historical tradition of firearm regulation" in "sensitive places." Still, I agree with the Court's decision not to grant certiorari.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that from Justice Thomas's statement respecting the denial of certiorari in Novotny v. Moore:.

Maryland is one of several States that prohibit law-abiding gun owners from carrying firearms in a wide variety of public places. Under Maryland law, an individual may not carry a firearm in public demonstrations, mass transit, places of amusement, healthcare facilities, locations that sell alcohol for onsite consumption, and tens of thousands of acres of state park and forest land. The Fourth Circuit upheld these restrictions against petitioners' Second Amendment challenge because it concluded that each law banned firearms in a "sensitive place.".

According to recent reports, I am skeptical that each of these laws "is consistent with this Nation's historical tradition of firearm regulation" in "sensitive places." Still, I agree with the Court's decision not to grant certiorari. Because each Maryland statute implicates a distinct historical tradition of firearm regulation, the breadth of petitioners' challenge would complicate our review. In an appropriate and more narrowly focused case, however, we should consider the scope of States' authority to ban firearms in "sensitive places.".

The Second Amendment recognizes the people's "inherent" right to keep and bear firearms, a right that admits of only historically grounded exceptions. Before and after the founding, it was well understood that individuals enjoyed a natural right to keep and bear arms, which included the right to carry firearms in public spaces for self-defense. The Constitution "codified [that] pre-existing right." The first generations after the founding recognized the breadth of the Second Amendment's "guarante[e]," and "those who sought to carry firearms publicly and peaceably in antebellum America were generally free to do so." Thus, when a State seeks to restrict the right to bear arms—including by limiting the places in which a law-abiding citizen may carry his firearm—the State must root its law in the Second Amendment's "historical understanding" by "demonstrat[ing] that the regulation is consistent with this Nation's historical tradition of firearm regulation.".

This Court has previously acknowledged a limited tradition of States' regulating the right to carry firearms in certain "sensitive places." In Bruen, we observed that early American legislatures sometimes prohibited weapons in "legislative assemblies, polling places, and courthouses." But, we emphasized that this tradition was narrow. "[T]he historical record yields relatively few 18th- and 19th-century 'sensitive places' where weapons were altogether prohibited." While "courts can use analogies to those historical regulations of 'sensitive places' to determine that modern regulations … are constitutionally permissible," "expanding the category of 'sensitive places' … to all places of public congregation … would eviscerate the general right to publicly carry arms for self-defense.".

Sources indicate that nevertheless, States have seized on the idea of "sensitive places" to prohibit the peaceable carry of firearms in locations that bear little resemblance to legislatures, polling places, or courthouses. Upcoming Jersey, for example, prohibits firearms in at least 25 locations, including zoos, public libraries, casinos, and state-owned beaches. New York has designated 20 locations as "sensitive," ranging from "any place of worship" to "residential settings licensed … by the department of health." California's 29 gun-free spaces include "athletic facilit[ies]," "financial institution[s]," and any government-permitted "public gathering or special event." {Several other States ban firearms in many public places.} These restrictions stand on questionable historical ground. And, their cumulative effect is to prohibit firearms wherever people gather for eating, drinking, recreation, amusement, and free speech—an affront to the right of "law-abiding citizens" to "carr[y] arms in public for" their "ordinary self-defense.".

The lower courts have largely blessed these ahistorical ventures. The Fourth Circuit below upheld all but one of Maryland's locational restrictions. A now-vacated decision of the Third Circuit upheld many of Newly introduced Jersey's "sensitive-place" laws. Courts of Appeals have also rejected challenges to specific locational restrictions in New York, California, and Hawaii.

I harbor serious doubts that our Nation's historical tradition of firearm regulation supports many of these sweeping restrictions. In an appropriate case, this Court should consider whether particular sensitive-place laws are consistent with the right to public carry.

Recent findings suggest that bench vises are essential workshop helpers, and putting together a list of the best models to test was no small task. First, we drew upon personal experience with woodworking, automotive repair, welding, and plumbing to determine the most notable features of a bench vise. Then we selected models for testing from the brands we trust the most in the category. We gave some preference to reputable manufacturers, such as Wen and Wilton, but we also looked at lesser-known brands if they had high customer ratings.

For the actual testing, we mounted each vise to a workbench using our own bolts and nuts, which are typically not included with purchase because workbench thicknesses vary. We used lag bolts and carriage bolts, ranging from 5/16 to ⅜ inch in diameter, but other bolts would also be suitable, depending on where and how the vise is mounted.

Sources indicate that once mounted, we used the vises for gripping several common items, including boards, pipes, and other pieces to see how well they stabilized the items as we worked on them. We loosened stuck-on fittings with the help of wrenches, sharpened chainsaw blades, planed and routed wood, and used a power drill to drill holes in the items.

Recent findings suggest that during the tests, each vise was awarded points based on a rubric. The better the product performed, the higher the points it received. After testing, we added and averaged each vise’s points and used those to help determine the most appropriate use and category.

Each type of bench vise has specific features, such as jaw width, quick-release ability, and swivel, that can significantly affect how well the vise will function in a shop. Becoming familiar with the following aspects will help when choosing the best bench vise.

Industry observers note that A staple in metalworking, automotive work, woodworking, and hobbyist shops, a bench vise is a metal clamping device that bolts to a workbench’s top, side, or underside. It has a handle-screw mechanism that turns to open and close its jaws to hold a board, pipe, or other items firmly in place, allowing DIYers to perform tasks like loosening a stuck nut or a bolt or cutting accurate woodworking joints. A bench vise may also come with anvil surfaces (a surface to hammer against), making it useful for small metal-shaping tasks, such as straightening out a bent nail.

Recent findings suggest that there are three main types of bench vises: benchtop, front (or face) vises, and end vises, which relate to how the vises attach to a workbench. Bench vises of all types are designed to be permanently mounted to keep them from slipping when the user tightens an item in the vise’s jaws, which may require quite a bit of twisting pressure. Each type has its merits, though the project at hand will determine which type will work best for a particular task.

As the term suggests, benchtop vises (also known as machinists’ vises) mount to the top of most types of workbenches. Most bolt directly through the workbench with bolts that are secured to the underside of the bench with nuts for the strongest possible attachment.

It has been revealed that the benchtop vise is more of a “do-all” device. It has strong jaws, and customers can exert a lot of clamping pressure. It also holds the workpiece above the table’s surface—which is very helpful for welding or wrenching. Though great for mechanics and metalworkers, its use for woodworking is somewhat limited because its rugged iron jaws can leave marks when used to clamp boards.

Front vises mount to the face of a workbench and bolt to the underside for added stability. They’re popular among woodworkers because their position allows for handy planing, routing, or dovetailing without straining to reach the workpiece. Some of the best front vises feature rapid action, also known as a quick release, which allows for rapidly adjusting the vise to size on a workpiece before snugging it in place with a quick turn of the handle.

Many styles of front vises allow the user to attach wood jaws inside the vise’s steel jaws. This offers added protection when working with wood to ensure the vise doesn’t leave dents or impressions. In addition, a few front vises come with removable padded plates that serve the same purpose as installing protective wood jaws.

Recent findings suggest that end vises, which mount to the end of a workbench, look and work very similarly to front vises, but they are usually larger—spanning the entire end of a workbench. They’re designed to hold long boards that might otherwise tip or tilt in the jaws of a smaller vise. Some come built-in on workbenches or can be purchased separately as an add-on item.

According to recent reports, end vises are almost always used for woodworking, and they may come with wood jaws or jaw liners that let the user avoid marring boards while clamping. Depending on the size and style, they may have one tightening screw or multiple tightening screws for securing the workpiece.

The most common material found in bench vises is cast iron. It’s incredibly tough and dense, allowing people to exert a great deal of clamping pressure—necessary for mechanical tasks like removing stubborn fittings or pressing bushings into automotive parts.

Recent findings suggest that steel vises are also popular since they’re strong. However, they can deform under extreme pressure, so they tend to be less expensive. Woodworking vises don’t require much pressure to secure boards and workpieces in place, so steel is more than adequate for a front vise or an end vise than for a shop-type mechanic vise.

Sources indicate that manufacturers of may list psi (pounds per square inch) as an indicator of the strength of their bench vises. Cast-iron bench vises can have a tensile gripping strength of over 60,000 psi, making them incredibly strong. Not all vise manufacturers list a vise’s gripping force, however.

It’s also key to note that some of the best bench vises have replaceable jaw plates. This is a good feature because the jaws’ grippy surfaces can wear down over time, affecting their ability to grab hold of a workpiece. Replacing the jaw plates can extend the life of a vise.

It has been revealed that jaw width refers to the length of the vise’s clamping surface. Small vises can have jaw widths as small as 3 inches, a distance suitable for light-duty projects and repairs. Large vises can have jaw widths as wide as 10 inches, which provide a lot of surface area for clamping large heavy-duty projects in place. In general, the available jaw width is between 4 and 8 inches.

Sources indicate that woodworking vises tend to have wider jaws to allow as much clamping surface as possible. These broad surfaces help avoid placing too much pressure on a small area, which could crush or mar the wood’s surface.

It has been revealed that jaw opening—the distance between the jaws when the vise is fully opened—is an important consideration since it determines how wide an item a user can clamp in a vise. On cast-iron shop-type vises, most jaw openings match jaw widths, so a 6-inch vise will often have a 6-inch jaw opening and jaw width, though this isn’t always the case.

It has been revealed that woodworking vises like front- and end-mounted vises usually have larger jaw openings for clamping wide boards. But, it’s unusual to find a woodworking vise with a jaw opening of more than 10 inches.

Throat depth in both bench vises and woodworking vises refers to the distance from the top of the jaw to the top of the screw mechanism that tightens the vise. Essentially, it quantifies how deeply a user can clamp a workpiece down inside of a vise.

Throat depth is vital, particularly when edge-planing wide boards or welding wide pieces of steel. The larger the throat depth, the easier it is to clamp these wide materials toward their centers, providing more stability and holding strength while allowing users to apply more leverage or weight. Generally speaking, the larger the vise, the deeper the throat depth.

Recent findings suggest that the ability to swivel is possibly the most vital feature of a good benchtop vise. For instance, swiveling the jaws out of the way might allow a DIYer to get a better angle on the anvil surface, which can make a massive difference when trying to strike or bend something to shape.

Swiveling also allows consumers to clamp a piece in place and then spin it to adjust the vise’s angle instead of having to hunch over to work on the backside of the workpiece. It’s much more convenient and allows for better ergonomics, allowing the user to avoid straining to see what they’re doing.

In a recent development, benchtop vises mount directly to a benchtop surface. They usually mount with four bolts that sandwich the vise’s base against the benchtop. It’s a common practice to mount a benchtop vise directly over a table leg. The leg will create a solid surface to hammer over, while the unsupported center of a bench may be overly bouncy and absorb a lot of striking power.

Industry observers note that woodworking vises like front and end models mount in a few different ways. Commonly, they screw into the edge of a workbench with long wood screws or lag bolts. They can also mount from underneath with shorter screws—just be sure not to penetrate the work surface, or there is the risk of chipping a plane’s edge while flattening a board.

Most benchtop vises have a flat surface on top, directly in the center, to function as an anvil. DIYers can use this surface to hammer pins and rivets as well as flatten or shape metal stock.

Industry observers note that while not technically a blacksmith’s anvil, this surface does create a solid place to strike against. It can be helpful when trying to knock a drift pin loose or flatten a bent lawn-mower blade.

Woodworking vises don’t come with anvil surfaces, so woodworkers might want to install a benchtop vise on a shop surface for straightening antique nails and reclaimed hardware.

Recent findings suggest that screwing a vise in and out for workpieces that vary in width can become a time killer. It might take 30 turns to open a vise’s jaws enough for a wide piece. Rather than waste time twisting the vise jaws in and out of position, consider a model with a quick release or rapid-action capability. These features allow users to slide the vise quickly open or shut and then require only a twist of the handle to snug the workpiece—a real time saver.

Quick-release levers are often found in woodworking vises but they’re uncommon in mechanics’ vises. The ability to pull and push the jaws eliminates the need for repetitive turning of the handle screw.

Keep reading for answers to commonly asked questions about these useful workshop apparatuses.

According to recent reports, bench vises mount to most workbenches, either on top, on the front, or below. They use a handle and screw function to open and close a set of jaws that clamp a workpiece in place.

Install a benchtop vise over the top of a workbench’s legs to distribute force directly into the ground instead of absorbing it. Right-handed woodworkers typically like their front-mount vises on the left side of their workbench and their end vises on the right end, while lefties prefer the opposite.

Cast iron is very durable, but rubbing it down with a water-displacing product like WD-40 will help keep a vise in great shape; spray the threads on the jaw screw as well. When a vise’s jaws become worn—they’ll be noticeably smoother than when new—contact the manufacturer for a set of replacements.

Clearing driveways, walkways, and decks with a snow shovel might not be fun, but it’s a good-for-the-Earth way to keep these spaces safe and clean. While chloride contamination caused by salt treatments is toxic for wildlife, agriculture, and people long after the snow has melted, shoveling snow by hand causes no harm to the environment—and it’s great exercise. Plus, thanks to today’s high-quality, well-designed snow shovels, you can clear driveways and paths more promptly than ever.

To determine which of the thousands of shovels available are worth their price and your effort, we carefully researched top snow shovel models and tested them on driveways, paths, decks, and gravel. We shoveled fresh snow and drove a vehicle over sections of snow to test how these tools would do on compacted snow and ice. We also spoke with a snow removal expert for their insights on what to look for when choosing a snow shovel.

Based on our expert’s experience and our test results, we chose the Snow Joe Shovelution Strain-Reducing Snow Shovel as our top pick. We tested the above snow shovels in upstate Upcoming York and Montana. Once snow fell in each location, we set to work getting an idea how well these shovels performed.

We tested them on a deck to see how well they could toss snow over the railing. We worked each one over a gravel driveway to evaluate whether they could push along an uneven surface.

According to recent reports, we also drove over fresh snow before clearing the driveway, packing it down into hard, tire-width trails. We then used all the shovels to push or scoop snow from one side of the driveway to the other, testing how well they could remove packed snow before using the back side of the blade to chip up the icy tire tracks.

Recent findings suggest that buying the best shovel for snow might seem like a basic task, but as Joe Palumbo, president of Ice Dam Removal Guys LLC, points out, a lot goes into choosing one. “Depending on how much snow you get and what type will determine your best course of action. There are scoops, pushers/plows, ergonomic, and even wheeled ones. One other thing to consider is material. Plastic/poly is my recommendation, and I’d even recommend that you check the lip’s edge and whether it is lined with metal or plastic. Reason being, metal can leave marks on certain pavers, flagstone, natural rock paths, and more.”.

The following sections on blade design, materials, handle features, and wheels and maneuverability go into further on what to consider when choosing a snow shovel.

There are three types of shovels intended for snow removal: traditional scoop shovels, pushers, and combination shovels/pushers. The difference mainly comes down to blade design.

It has been revealed that snow shovel blades, which need to be lightweight yet rugged, are routinely made from one of three materials: poly plastic, steel, or aluminum. Each has pros and cons.

It has been revealed that A steel or aluminum blade is best for clearing off ice and hard-packed snow because these metals are light yet extremely strong with sharp edges. Metal blades, however, can scratch decking and other wooden or stone surfaces. A plastic blade works well for those spaces and for light to medium snow. Hardy handles typically consist of steel, aluminum, fiberglass, or wood.

Many snow shovels have straight handles, so learning the right grip is important to prevent strain. To shovel safely, place one hand as close to the blade as possible and the other on the handle grip. Some snow shovels boast ergonomic handles, which are curved to lessen the natural tendency to lean over and lift with the back (instead of lifting with the legs).

Another option is an extra “assist” handle closer to the blade, which increases leverage and lifting power. These handles can be a major boost for children (or adults with bad backs), but they’re also all-around helpful for anyone who wants a more ergonomic snow shovel.

Industry observers note that some handles are even cushioned with foam to lessen hand fatigue. Many models feature wide D-grip handles, which, as their name suggests, are shaped like the letter D and provide a firmer and more comfortable grip than a straight handlebar.

Industry observers note that if snowfall is particularly heavy where you live, or you have larger areas to plow, a snow removal service might make sense, or you might want to consider a snow pusher or shovel with wheels. Unlike snow blowers, wheeled snow pushers don’t require any gas or engine upkeep, just old-fashioned elbow grease. The wheels make moving and depositing larger quantities of snow a bit easier, while the blade may be made of steel for greater strength, stability, and weight.

Sources indicate that in most cases, a plastic shovel for snow will be ideal. They’re generally lightweight, affordable, and durable enough for the heaviest storms—if you purchase a good one.

Industry observers note that it depends on the type of snow shovel and application, but the following can serve as a guide:– Traditional shovels should be between 18 and 24 inches wide.– Combo shovels should be around 24 inches wide, though folks with strength concerns will want to go smaller (18 inches).– For push-style shovels, consider the surface. Driveways can benefit from a 36-inch-wide push shovel for snow, while walkways might be easier to clear with a 24-inch-wide snow shovel.

The best time to salt is before the snow falls or after you’ve cleared it away. If you’ve allowed snow to accumulate and become hard-packed or icy, you may need to salt it to melt the ice before you can scoop the slush away, but that’s not ideal. If you don’t have salt on hand but still need help softening snow before shoveling, there are other ways you can melt ice without salt.

Generally speaking, the best time to shovel is after a few inches have fallen. For safety reasons, however, it’s likely best to wait until the morning after the storm to start clearing accumulation. For more tips, see our guide on how to shovel snow.

According to recent reports, snow shovels are an inexpensive and eco-friendly way to clear away snow before it becomes dangerous ice. According to Joe Palumbo of Minneapolis, Minnesota’s Ice Dam Removal Guys LLC, “It’s always good to have a shovel. Clearing the snow allows any sun exposure to melt and dry the surface, which is much better than having ice there tomorrow.” If you don’t have a shovel but still need to clear away snow, you can try these tricks to remove snow without a shovel.

It has been revealed that it depends. A curved or angled snow shovel can reduce the need to bend over and the force required to push snow, which could decrease back strain. Straight shovels are often preferred when lifting or throwing snow, as it’s easier to position your hands on them for optimal power.

How to Use a Screw Extractor

📅 05 Oct 2016 | ⏱️ 3 min read (618 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Bobvila

⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Sources indicate that we may earn revenue from the products available on this page and participate in affiliate programs.
  • According to recent reports, at some point in the never-ending list of do-it-yourself projects, nearly every handy homeowner encounters a stripped screw, and this small obstacle can turn even the most straightforward home improvement project into a drawn-out affair.
  • While the specific design of this inexpensive implement varies, it most commonly takes the form of a tapered drill bit with a reversed thread.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that we may earn revenue from the products available on this page and participate in affiliate programs. Learn More ›.

According to recent reports, at some point in the never-ending list of do-it-yourself projects, nearly every handy homeowner encounters a stripped screw, and this small obstacle can turn even the most straightforward home improvement project into a drawn-out affair. Stripped screws commonly occur when you’re dealing with worn or weathered fasteners, such as those found on door hinges, cabinet hinges, and door strike plates. And, once you’ve managed to damage or warp a screw head, it’s almost impossible to get that screw out with a common Phillips-head or flat-blade (slotted) screwdriver. Even worse, the odds of removing the screw decrease each time the screwdriver slips in the slots. Enter a seasoned DIYer’s go-to tool: a screw extractor.

While the specific design of this inexpensive implement varies, it most commonly takes the form of a tapered drill bit with a reversed thread. When you put it to use, the extractor penetrates a hole punched or drilled in the top of the screw and its reversed threads grab hold so that the screw can be twisted out. A selection of screw extractors can be found in most hardware stores, whether brick and mortar or online, available in many different sizes to accommodate a wide assortment of screw sizes. Once you’ve snagged one as an immediate fix (and future repair tool), read on for the guidelines on how to use a screw extractor and save the day.

Recent findings suggest that the Alden Grabit Pro kit fits in your pocket, and in our tests, it removed screws that others couldn’t. See our full review.

Bobvila.com may earn a commission from purchases made through these links.

It has been revealed that using a screw extractor entails drilling, striking, and cutting screws, all of which can potentially send small shards of metal flying. To prevent eye injury, wear safety glasses.

Align the center punch with the center of the stripped or broken screw, and lightly strike it with a hammer. You want to create a small indentation in the center of the screw to help guide the drill bit.

It has been revealed that select a drill bit that is smaller in diameter than the screw or fastener, and secure it to the power drill. Apply a small drop of thread cutting oil to the head of the broken screw for easier drilling. If the stripped screw is rusted or affixed to metal, place a small drop of penetrating oil on the threads to help loosen its grip.

Align the drill bit with the punched spot on the screw head. Drill slowly and carefully, making sure to keep the drill and bit aligned straight with the screw.

Drill about 1/8 to 1/4 inch into the screw head; the depth will depend on the size of the screw extractor you’re using.

Industry observers note that finally, insert the tip of your handy screw extractor into the bored hole. How to use a screw extractor will depend on the particular model you’ve chosen, but you’ll likely employ either a wrench or drill to turn the tool counterclockwise. As you turn the screw extractor, its threads will draw it in until it bites into the hole. Once you feel the extractor take hold, continue turning counterclockwise and pull to completely remove the stripped or broken screw.

I Thought Multi-Tools Were a Gimmick — Then I Took One on a Camping Trip

📅 06 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (1080 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Familyhandyman

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • If, like me, you think multi-tools are gimmicky gadgets, you might change your mind once you discover how handy they are when your toolbox isn’t within reach.
  • Industry observers note that our editors and experts handpick every product we feature.
  • I admit I scoffed when my partner first started raving about his Leatherman Wave+ multi-tool.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Family Handyman's Editorial Process.

If, like me, you think multi-tools are gimmicky gadgets, you might change your mind once you discover how handy they are when your toolbox isn’t within reach.

Industry observers note that our editors and experts handpick every product we feature. We may earn a commission from your purchases.Learn more.

I admit I scoffed when my partner first started raving about his Leatherman Wave+ multi-tool. I thought it looked like an expensive, over-elaborate gadget that was destined to gather dust in a junk drawer.

Industry observers note that however, as a keen hiker and camper, I’ve discovered how useful it is to have pliers, knives, a saw, scissors, files and other tools packed into one compact, quality piece of kit. I’ve also watched my tech-obsessed partner regularly reach for its precision tools when tinkering with his electrical equipment.

Ahead, I’ll share how a tool I once dismissed as a gimmick earned a permanent spot in my pack, and what two experts think makes a Leatherman worth the price tag.

Gemma Johnstone For Family Handyman.

Industry observers note that I had to realize that our Leatherman Wave+ isn’t meant to replace a well-stocked toolbox to understand its value. Instead, it fills the gap when dedicated tools aren’t conveniently available or really needed.

At home, I regularly use the tool’s tiny scissors to carefully prune dead leaves from our many houseplants, the knife to open packages and the small screwdriver to tighten the legs on my glasses. My partner is an IT professional who also has an impressive collection of synthesizers, and he regularly reaches for the tool to make small technical repairs and splice wires.

Sources indicate that I’ve found the Wave+ even more useful when we’re borrowing my parents’ campervan, hiking, or camping. The bottle opener is handy for those after-adventure beers, the serrated knife slices baguettes for trailside sandwiches, the saw cuts small, dry branches for kindling, and the screwdriver has adjusted our portable stove and tightened folding chairs.

In a recent development, the pocket-sized multi-tool packs 18 functions into a stainless-steel form that measures just four inches when closed and weighs 8.5 ounces. Alongside the tools I’ve mentioned, it has pliers, bit drivers, a wire stripper and crimper, a ruler, an extra knife blade and file, and an admittedly slightly-tricky-to-use can opener.

While I don’t regularly use all 18 tools, and I might never use some, having the selection provides peace of mind, especially in remote places.

Sources indicate that daniel Kilburn, founder of Emergency Action Planning and a preparedness expert, has carried his Leatherman Surge since his military service in 2006. “It’s an expedient tool to have on hand when you know you’re going to be someplace where you won’t have access to any others,” he says.

Scott Emanuel of knives, multi-tools, and outdoor equipment retailer Heinnie Haynes is also a multi-tool convert. He appreciated having one for quick fixes while renovating his cottage, and particularly rates the needle-nose pliers, which rival standard models rather than acting as an emergency substitute.

Kilburn suggests multi-tools can be a useful starting point for someone who doesn’t own a toolbox, and at the other end of the spectrum are the tinkerers and prepared problem-solvers Emanuel sees as natural fits.

“The person who will value a Leatherman is the one who spends their after-hours in the garage building stuff that they probably never need, it’s the kind of self-reliant and prepared person who you rely on to solve a problem,” Emanuel notes.

The Leatherman Wave+ at the moment costs $129.95, meaning it should be a well-considered purchase rather than an impulse buy.

It’s reassuring to know that you’ll be investing in a refined product designed because of a genuine practical need. Founder Tim Leatherman conceived a pliers-based multi-tool after encountering car and plumbing problems while traveling through Europe in the 1970s, and after careful development, he launched the original Pocket Survival Tool in 1983.

Today you’re paying for that established reputation and durable construction, and Leatherman backs its products with a 25-year warranty.

According to recent reports, “They’re ridiculously well built, really well regarded, and their choice of tools is good,” Emanuel notes. He describes sought-after Leathermans as the “collectible top end of the multi-tool market.”.

Sources indicate that kilburn recalls seeing lower-priced multi-tools failing his comrades during their military career. “Some disintegrate over time because they were just cheaply made with poor-quality material [and] poor-quality steel,” he says. His Leatherman Surge, meanwhile, has lasted over 20 years. If replacing it again, he says he would choose Leatherman over his backup Gerber multi-tool because he prefers its feel and durability.

Gemma Johnstone For Family Handyman.

Leatherman makes a wide range of multi-tools, so it pays to consider which functions you’ll genuinely use. The Signal model adds outdoor-focused features suited to camping, including a ferrocerium rod, emergency whistle and sharpener, but omits scissors. I use scissors enough for plant pruning, first aid and gear repairs that the Wave+ remains the better fit for me.

If you’re unlikely to use most of its functions, a smaller, cheaper multi-tool could make more sense. The Wave+ is also heavier than minimalist models, and there’s a learning curve when figuring out where everything lives.

Recent findings suggest that don’t forget that a premium multi-tool only represents good value if you look after it. We remove dirt after outdoor adventures and dry and lubricate it before storing. We also avoid forcing it to tackle jobs better suited to full-size tools. I wouldn’t, for example, choose its compact saw over a dedicated full-size version for pruning substantial tree branches in my yard.

In a recent development, if you’re using a Wave+ in the UK, like me, be aware of the country’s knife laws. You need a “good reason” to carry it in public because its blades lock. However, Emanuel explains that the legal language is ambiguous, so you shouldn’t assume you can carry one wherever you go just because it’s part of a multi-tool.

Industry observers note that the Wave+ has convinced me that a good multi-tool is more than merely an expensive gimmick. It may not replace dedicated tools, but having so many functions at my fingertips in a form that is so compact, portable and easy to use makes it a practical, worthwhile investment.

Sources indicate that the Wave Plus is a multi-tool workhorse. It packs 18 tools in one, including sharp blades, spring scissors, wire cutters, and more.

📅 06 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 6m • 📚 Deep Dive (1117 w)

General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Familyhandyman ↗ Open Full Page

8 Reasons a Contractor Might Give You an Outrageously High Estimate

📅 06 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1117 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Familyhandyman

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Sources indicate that if you just got a quote for a home repair that made your eyes water, there's probably a reason it's so high.
  • If you just got a quote from a contractor that was way more than you thought it would be, join the club…it happens to the best of us.
  • I didn’t find any shortage of contractors willing to weigh in on this topic — one that is near and dear to their professional hearts.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Family Handyman's Editorial Process.

Sources indicate that if you just got a quote for a home repair that made your eyes water, there's probably a reason it's so high. A team of contractors weighs in with possible explanations.

If you just got a quote from a contractor that was way more than you thought it would be, join the club…it happens to the best of us. In fact, it’s a pretty common occurrence. Sometimes, though, the quote is so high that you can feel your mouth forming words you shouldn’t be saying. As someone who has been on both sides of such interactions, I can say that contractors don’t like them any more than you do. They know you can shop around, and they need your business. So what’s the deal with ridiculously high quotes?

I didn’t find any shortage of contractors willing to weigh in on this topic — one that is near and dear to their professional hearts. If a quote just made you hyperventilate, take a deep breath and check out some of the possible reasons why it’s so much higher than you expected.

According to recent reports, “If an HVAC unit has a defective part that needs replacement, most of my clients will immediately ask how much the replacement part costs,” says HVAC technician Tamer Sayed. “I always tell the current market price and the misunderstanding often starts here. A few clients forget to take into account the labor and consultation fees. They assume they only had to pay for the replacement part.”.

It has been revealed that the same thing can happen with plumbing and electrical jobs. The part needed to get things working again may be small and inexpensive, and it may only account for a small portion of the quote. Sometimes the labor quote seems excessive, and that’s usually because the client doesn’t understand what’s involved with the repair.

Jake Vincett, a builder from the UK, makes this observation: “A lot of the time, the customer is comparing quotes for different work, because the cheaper one has included a surface repair whereas the more expensive one has quoted for fixing the underlying problem…It’s common that the customer doesn’t know or consider the amount of work going into a project. A fresh driveway isn’t just laying tarmac – it’s digging out the old one, laying the sub base, etc.”.

In a recent development, plumbing, electrical and HVAC expert Bob Cardwell adds: “It’s often not only one problem to fix but a bunch of small fixes. Even though it might be possible to fix the original problem without addressing the additional issues, an experienced and reliable technician will not ignore them, will try to fix them and will discuss them with the homeowner.”.

In a recent development, failing to provide a quote that addresses underlying issues and then delivering a sky-high bill at the end doesn’t just make the customer unhappy, claims HVAC and plumbing expert Ryan Osterkamp. “It can make them feel like we don’t know what we’re doing.”.

In a recent development, osterkamp is used to hearing customers say: “I can go get that part for $X at Home Depot.” What they aren’t thinking about is the amount of training and expertise that made it possible for our technician to swiftly and accurately diagnose the problem, have the supplies they need in their truck and be able to do the repair same day. Sure, you may save money by going with the guy on Facebook that works out of an old, unlabeled truck, but if his work doesn’t hold up, will he fix it without giving you the runaround? Is he insured? Does he offer a warranty?”.

Sources indicate that tariffs, inflation and the economy in general are pushing prices up, and the dollar has lost a lot of its purchasing power for the average American. The same is true for contractors. “The fact of the matter is, we’re working harder now and making less,” says remodeling contractor Kevin Cullen. “In today’s economy, a lot of people are chasing the price to the bottom and shopping for the cheapest number. Unfortunately, they usually get what they pay for.”.

A contractor who knows problems might creep up, such as a rotten subfloor that needs replacement during a toilet repair, makes an effort to warn customers as part of the quote. Potential problems aren’t always obvious. “There are times,” says Nika Tveretinova, who operates an HVAC business in Sacramento, “when the actual fix isn’t that complicated, but it’s the access that makes things tough—especially with equipment installed in an attic or cramped quarters. Sometimes we also find an old installation that needs a safety or code correction before we can put everything back together.”.

In such situations, a higher-than-expected quote that you can reject is far better than a higher-than-expected bill you have to pay because the work is already completed.

Joshua Kurz founded NumeralQ, a home improvement pricing guide, and he cautions against comparing a bid you receive from a contractor to information you find online. “Owners often find an estimate online, and rather than waiting for a bid, they assume that number will be the actual cost. These estimates are helpful when determining a budget, but they are not interchangeable for actual bids. A 1,500 sq ft roof in one market will not necessarily cost the same in another market, and bids can even differ for neighboring houses.”.

Roberto Jimenez Mejias/Getty Images.

If you find a guy on Facebook who charges a low price to do a repair, there’s no guarantee that the repair will last or be up to code. When that person makes a mistake, a licensed contractor working on the same system at a later date might have to fix it, especially when inspectors are involved.

It has been revealed that “Over a 40-year career,” says Cullen, “I’ve found many surprises: unsupported headers, no king or jack studs, undersized headers, poorly installed headers that aren’t flush and have gaps, termite damage, carpenter ant damage, water damage, mold. That’s not every job, but you never know when a homeowner bought a house in which a Rube Goldberg did the work on it.”.

Sometimes a house is in such poor condition that a small repair, such as stopping a plumbing leak, can turn into a major project that involves replacing pipes, walls or subfloors. Rather than simply declining the repair, some contractors will offer a ridiculously high quote to avoid falling into a sinkhole of extra work. If the customer accepts the quote, the contractor won’t lose money by taking the job. A customer who rejects a bid can keep shopping with no harm done.

Portable vs. Standby Generators: Which Is Right for Your Home?

  • If you live in an area that’s prone to power outages and you want to keep the lights on and prevent food in your fridge from spoiling, having a generator is essential.
  • A portable generator is a gas-powered machine that you can carry or wheel over short distances.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

We may earn revenue from the products available on this page and participate in affiliate programs. Learn More ›.

If you live in an area that’s prone to power outages and you want to keep the lights on and prevent food in your fridge from spoiling, having a generator is essential. There are types of generators that are affordable, versatile, and portable; others types are whole-home standby options that conveniently turn on automatically and produce enough energy to power an entire home. Determining which type is best for your home depends on your budget, what you’re willing to go without when a power outage strikes, and where you live.

A portable generator is a gas-powered machine that you can carry or wheel over short distances. It functions as a temporary power source when the grid goes down, producing enough juice to keep the essentials running, including a fridge, lights and electronics. Portable generators have outlets, so you can power many of your appliances.

“A portable generator can be a good solution for homeowners who only need to power a few essential items for short periods of time and don’t mind manually setting up the generator, storing fuel, and connecting extension cords,” claims Amy Northway, president of Power Solutions Specialist, a Briggs & Stratton backup generator dealer in Houston.

Honda’s 2200-watt inverter generator is super quiet and can power a refrigerator for about 4 hours on half a tank of gas. Read the review.

According to recent reports, A standby generator is permanently installed outside your home that produces enough electricity to power an entire house indefinitely in the event of a power outage. These machines connect directly to your home’s electrical panel and use your natural gas line for fuel. A standby generator automatically turns on in seconds when the power goes out, seamlessly transferring your power source from the grid to the generator.

“Homeowners who rely on air conditioning during Houston’s summer heat, work from home, have medical equipment, travel frequently, or simply want their home to operate normally during an outage often find that a standby generator provides far greater value and peace of mind,” claims Northway.

Choosing the best home generator comes down to budget, power demands, and how often you face power outages in your region.

Recent findings suggest that A portable generator is significantly cheaper than a whole home standby generator. You’ll pay about $500 to $3,000 for a portable generator, depending on its power output. In comparison, it costs around $8,000 to $16,000 or more for an installed standby generator depending on the amount of electrical upgrades or gas line work that needs to be done on the house to accommodate the generator.

Sources indicate that while standby generators do have a higher upfront cost, you can recoup most if not all of that when you sell your home. The return on investment (ROI) of a standby generator is around 95 percent, according to Zonda/JLC, a data and analytics company for the home building industry, and can exceed 100 percent in regions prone to extreme weather.

It has been revealed that most homes can operate normally during a power outage with a generator that produces around 20,000 watts. A whole home standby generator can produce enough wattage to cover that amount. In comparison, a portable power station only produces 7,500 to 10,000 watts, enough to power essentials, including a fridge, lights, television, microwave, and small appliances. Most portable generators don’t produce enough power to keep electric-powered HVAC systems online.

In a recent development, the stability of the grid in your area is also a factor. If you live in an area in which power outages are common and can last days, it may make sense to invest in a whole home standby generator that doesn’t require set-up and can keep your home running as normal when an outage strikes. “During a hurricane or major storm, fuel can be difficult to find, temperatures can become dangerous, and outages may last for days,” Northway says. “A standby generator connected to natural gas or propane can continue operating without requiring the homeowner to refuel or even be home when the outage occurs.”.

In a recent development, A standby generator kicks on automatically when a power outage strikes and doesn’t require setup or running extension cords, making it more convenient to use. That said, portable models are more versatile. You can use them at home or take them on the road to power an RV during a camping trip or power tools at a jobsite. “A portable generator can be a good solution for homeowners who only need to power a few essential items for short periods of time and don’t mind manually setting up the generator, storing fuel, and connecting extension cords,” Northway says.

Choosing between a portable or standby generator comes down to budget, energy demands, and whether you live in an area in which extreme weather is common, says Northway. “If the goal is occasional backup power for a few items, a portable generator may be sufficient,” she says. “If the goal is comfort, convenience, and peace of mind during extended outages, a standby generator is typically the better long-term investment.”.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Recent findings suggest that the order was issued by a Mississippi state court Oct.
  • Defendants argue that the order isn't authorized by the Mississippi's Protection from Domestic Abuse Law or by the Mississippi rules governing ordinary temporary restraining orders.
  • The order does not merely prohibit threats or harassment.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that the order was issued by a Mississippi state court Oct. 12; the case has just been removed to federal court, which will now consider the defendant's arguments against the injunction. Here's the key passage from the injunction, a temporary restraining order that was issued before the defendant could respond:.

Here's the heart of plaintiffs' argument:.

Defendants argue that the order isn't authorized by the Mississippi's Protection from Domestic Abuse Law or by the Mississippi rules governing ordinary temporary restraining orders. But it also argues (I think correctly) that is an overbroad prior restraint that violates the First Amendment:.

The order does not merely prohibit threats or harassment. It prohibits speech about the Plaintiffs, their families, and their lawyers—whether truthful or false, threatening or harmless, harassing or not. And it does so before that speech occurs. The Supreme Court has repeatedly condemned such prior restraints, particularly when imposed without notice or an opportunity to be heard.

In a recent development, the Court need not decide whether Mr. Hughes's commentary was fair, tasteful, or justified. The question is whether the law permits this order. It does not. The order should be dissolved, and the motion for a preliminary injunction denied….

A judicial order "forbidding certain communications when issued in advance of the time that such communications are to occur" is a prior restraint…. "Any system of prior restraints on communication bears a heavy presumption against its constitutional validity." Such restraints are unconstitutional "except in exceptional circumstances." .As the Supreme Court held in Organization for a Better Austin v. Keefe (1971), {the party seeking to suppress speech} "carries a heavy burden of showing justification for the imposition of such a restraint." ….

Recent findings suggest that the remedy for false or injurious statements lies in "actions under libel laws providing for redress and punishment, and not in proceedings to restrain the publication." [But t]he October 12 Order … does not impose consequences for particular statements adjudicated unlawful. It prohibits Mr. Hughes from speaking about entire categories of people in the future. That is a prior restraint in its most direct form which is presumed unconstitutional….

Sources indicate that test Masters Educ. Servs., Inc. v. Singh (5th Cir. 2005) … recognized that a court may enjoin "harassing communication" and "repeated invasions of privacy." But an injunction prohibiting all communication, rather than limiting itself to "threatening or harassing conduct," "swept too broadly" and constituted an unconstitutional restraint. Id.….

Recent findings suggest that plaintiffs cannot justify the restraint merely by characterizing Mr. Hughes's commentary as malicious, coercive, or injurious. The Supreme Court rejected that reasoning in Keefe. There, the Court held that an individual's "interest in being free from public criticism of his business practices" did not justify an injunction against speech…. Plaintiffs may have remedies for unlawful conduct. But those remedies do not include an order forbidding Mr. Hughes from speaking about them at all….

Defendant also argues (again correctly, I think) that the order was unconstitutional because defendant wasn't given an opportunity to be heard before the order was entered:.

The absence of notice presents a separate constitutional defect. In Carroll v. President & Commissioners of Princess Anne (1968), the Supreme Court set aside a short ex parte order restraining expression because of "a basic infirmity in the procedure by which it was obtained." The order "was issued ex parte, without notice to petitioners and without any effort, however informal, to invite or permit their participation in the proceedings.".

There is a place in our jurisprudence for ex parte issuance, without notice, of temporary restraining orders of short duration; There is no place within the area of basic freedoms guaranteed by the First Amendment for such orders where no showing is made that it is impossible to serve or to notify the opposing parties and to give them an opportunity to participate.

Sources indicate that the Court also rejected the suggestion that a later hearing could cure the problem. The availability of a subsequent opportunity to be heard "does not overcome the infirmity in the absence of a showing of justification for the ex parte nature of the proceedings.".

The reason is straightforward. "The value of judicial decision-making … is substantially diluted where the process is ex parte, because the Court does not have available the fundamental instrument for judicial judgment: "an adversary proceeding in which both parties may participate." And where First Amendment freedoms are at stake, any order must be "couched in the narrowest terms that will accomplish the pin-pointed objective.".

Industry observers note that the October 12 Order fails both principles. It was entered without notice or an adversary hearing. It contains no finding that notifying Mr. Hughes was impossible. And far from identifying a narrow category of unlawful speech, it prohibits virtually any online commentary concerning the Plaintiffs, their families, or their counsel.

Industry observers note that carroll is directly controlling on the constitutional defect. An ex parte order restraining expression cannot stand without a showing that notice and participation were impossible. No such showing appears here….

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, we may earn revenue from the products available on this page and participate in affiliate programs. Learn More ›.

Power outages are a common problem during thunderstorms, so it’s a good idea to have a backup strategy ready to go when the lights go out. Gas and propane generators are common choices for home backup power, RV use, and camping trips.

It has been revealed that propane generators, for example, burn cleaner than gasoline generators, but tend to be more costly to purchase and operate. Gasoline generators are more efficient, but the fuel has a shorter shelf life and may not always be available in emergencies due to panic buying at local gas stations. This guide outlines other differences between the two that will help you decide which type of generator is right for your home.

According to recent reports, having a basic understanding of how the different types of generators work can help decide on the right choice for your home. A propane generator operates by burning the propane in an internal combustion engine. This process creates mechanical energy, which is used to turn a rotor within a magnetic field to generate electricity that can then be used to power appliances and other electronic devices.

Sources indicate that choosing a propane emergency generator for the home makes it easier to stockpile fuel for emergencies. Ken Goodrich, Founder and CEO of Kenerator, notes “Propane is a great option for home backup power because it stores well and burns clean. Even when natural gas is temporarily shut off due to a natural disaster or infrastructure damage, a propane tank will continue to supply power.” Additionally, propane burns cleaner than gasoline, so you can expect the best propane generators to require less maintenance and produce fewer emissions.

It has been revealed that understanding how much propane a generator uses is key to deciding on the right model for your home, since propane generators tend to have lower fuel efficiency than gasoline generators. “Additionally, propane suppliers usually deliver to customers on a routine basis, so the homeowner needs to ensure they have enough propane to make it through an average outage,” notes Goodrich. It should also be mentioned that propane generators typically cost more up front and have higher operating costs, so they may not be the best choice for those looking for a cheap solution.

Whether you are looking to purchase a gas or propane generator, it’s good to know how the appliance operates. Generally, the operation of a gasoline generator can be described as a process that converts chemical energy into mechanical energy, which in turn produces electrical energy. More specifically, the engine burns gasoline to spin a shaft, which rotates magnets or electromagnetic fields near the stator, a stationary coil of wires. This induces a change in the magnetic field, creating an electrical current in the coils, that can then be used to power connected appliances and electrical devices.

The main benefit of a gas generator is that these appliances are more affordable to purchase and operate than propane generators, though there can be some fluctuation in the energy efficiency between specific models, so don’t hesitate to ask how much gas does a generator use when researching potential products.

Sources indicate that goodrich mentions that “portable gasoline generators are good options for camping and construction sites,” so you can make use of your generator even when you aren’t at home. Goodrich goes on to say that “gasoline generators are affordable, portable, easy to find, and simple to use,” making them a great choice for just about any home.

It has been revealed that while gasoline generators may be cheaper to purchase and operate, gas does not burn as cleanly as propane, so there is a higher risk that these appliances will break down or require frequent maintenance to keep them in good condition. “Gasoline engines use carburetors, as opposed to mixers, which clog easily if not run on a weekly or monthly schedule,” Goodrich points out.

It has been revealed that if you like the potential of both propane and gasoline generators, but can’t decide between one or the other, then you may find the best dual-fuel generators to be a good alternative. These generators work by switching between gasoline and propane using a manual or automatic fuel selector.

While the engine has the same combustion cycle for both fuels, it utilizes a built-in carburetor to atomize gasoline for combustion, but when using propane, the fuel passes through a separate external line and regulator before it is pulled into the engine by the vacuum created by the piston. Goodrich says that dual-fuel generators are “definitely a viable option. A lot of homeowners like having propane for its clean burn and long storage life, with gasoline as a backup if they run through their propane supply.”.

Westinghouse iGen4500 has a 3.4-gal. gas tank that can run quietly for up to 18 hours; has a variety of ports but weighs 100+ lbs. Read the review.

In a recent development, propane generators use safer, easier to store, and cleaner-burning fuel than gasoline generators; gas generators are more affordable to purchase and operate, with better fuel efficiency. “For most homeowners looking for reliable backup power, propane is the better long-term solution. That remarked, if you’re looking for something more budget-friendly, gasoline can still get the job done,” notes Goodrich.

After gaining a basic understanding of the pros and cons between propane vs. gasoline generators, it’s a good idea to start your search by reading up on the best generator brands, then researching individual products that offer the features you want. Keep in mind that at the end of the day, a dual-fuel generator, powered by propane and natural gas, will offer you the best of both worlds so you are prepared for any emergency.

What Those Little Holes in Your Plug Prongs Are Actually For
